title: Hormones: the chemical messages behind alarm, growth and sleep

summary.text: Your heart can race while you sit perfectly still. You grow about half a centimetre a month, and you do not notice it happening. You get sleepy at nearly the same time each night. What is doing all this? In this lesson you will test whether pressure alone can speed up your pulse, find out how weak a taste your tongue can still pick up, and change the light in your evenings to see what happens to your sleepiness. You will meet the glands that send chemical messages through your blood, and find out why the same message gets different answers in different parts of you.
summary.art: A girl of ten sitting still on a chair with one hand on her chest and a surprised look, with small coloured dots travelling along faint blue lines inside her body outline from her neck, her kidneys and the middle of her head.

intro.hook: Think of the last time something gave you a fright. Maybe a pressure cooker whistled just behind you, or a dog barked, or a glass nearly slipped from your hand. Where in your body did you feel it? Point to every place. Then answer this: the fright was over in one second, so why did your heart keep thumping for a minute or more?
intro.text: Most people point to many places: the chest, the tummy, the hands, the legs, the mouth. That is odd. One small event changed many far-apart parts of you, almost together. And the thumping went on long after the danger had gone. Your body has two kinds of message. Nerve signals are fast and go to one place. Hormones are chemicals that travel more slowly, in the blood, and reach everywhere. In this lesson you look closely at hormones. You find out where hormones are made, how such tiny amounts can do so much, and how they control three things in your life: your alarm, your growth and your sleep.
intro.art: A steel pressure cooker letting out a jet of steam on a gas stove, and beside it a startled girl with her shoulders raised and her hands open.

outcomes: By the end I can point to the main endocrine glands on a body outline and name one hormone that each one makes.
By the end I can explain what adrenaline does in an alarm, why nerves start the alarm first, and why the alarm takes minutes to fade.
By the end I can explain why one hormone gets different answers from different cells, using the idea of receptors.
By the end I can describe how growth is controlled by growth hormone, thyroid hormone and the growth plates, and why growing stops.
By the end I can explain how a body clock, light and melatonin set the time I feel sleepy, and what sleep pressure adds.
By the end I can trace an order from the hypothalamus to the pituitary to another gland, and say why 'master gland' is only partly right.
By the end I can explain how hormones work in tiny amounts, and what doctors do when a gland makes too little.
By the end I can plan a fair test on my own body, repeat it, say what it shows and say honestly what it cannot show.

terms.meaning: A hormone is a chemical that some cells make and release, usually into the blood. It travels round the body and changes what certain other cells do.
terms.example: Adrenaline is a hormone. It leaves the adrenal glands, travels in the blood and makes the heart beat faster and harder.
terms.art: A small gland releasing tiny coloured dots into a red blood vessel, with the dots carried along towards a heart.

terms.meaning: A gland is a group of cells whose job is to make a substance and release it. Some glands release through a tube, as sweat glands and saliva glands do. Endocrine glands have no tube. They release straight into the blood.
terms.example: A saliva gland sends saliva down a tube into your mouth. The thyroid gland sends its hormone straight into the blood passing through it.
terms.art: Two glands side by side: one with a little tube leading to a surface, and one with no tube but with many small blood vessels running through it.

terms.meaning: The endocrine system is all the glands and cells that make hormones, taken together. 'Endocrine' comes from Greek words that mean 'to separate within', because the hormones are released inside the body.
terms.example: The pituitary, the thyroid, the adrenal glands, the pineal gland, parts of the pancreas, the ovaries and the testes all belong to the endocrine system.
terms.art: A child's body outline with eight small coloured glands marked from the head down to the hips.

terms.meaning: A receptor is a protein on or inside a cell that one kind of hormone fits. When the hormone joins the receptor, the receptor changes shape, and that starts changes inside the cell.
terms.example: Heart muscle cells carry receptors for adrenaline. A cell with no adrenaline receptor does not answer adrenaline at all.
terms.art: A close-up of a cell's outer skin with a cup-shaped protein in it and a small molecule settling into the cup.

terms.meaning: A target cell is any cell that has the receptor for a certain hormone, and so can answer that hormone.
terms.example: Liver cells are target cells for adrenaline. When adrenaline arrives, they release glucose into the blood.
terms.art: Many plain cells in a row and two cells among them coloured in, each with a small cup on its surface.

terms.meaning: The adrenal glands are two small flat glands, one sitting on top of each kidney. The inner part makes adrenaline. The outer part makes other hormones, such as cortisol.
terms.example: When you get a fright, nerves from your spinal cord signal the inner part of each adrenal gland, and adrenaline enters your blood within seconds.
terms.art: Two bean-shaped kidneys seen from the back, each with a small yellowish cap on top.

terms.meaning: Adrenaline is the hormone the adrenal glands release in an alarm or in hard exercise. It gets the body ready for sudden effort. It is also called epinephrine.
terms.example: Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster and harder, opens the airways in the lungs wider, and makes the liver release glucose.
terms.art: A girl sprinting from a barking dog, with small arrows pointing to her heart, lungs and leg muscles.

terms.meaning: The hypothalamus is a part of the brain about the size of an almond, low down in the middle. It is where the nervous system and the endocrine system meet. It is made of nerve cells, and some of those nerve cells release hormones.
terms.example: The hypothalamus sends 'releasing hormones' down a short stalk to the pituitary gland just below it.
terms.art: A brain cut down the middle, with an almond-sized part near the centre coloured in and a tiny stalk hanging from it.

terms.meaning: The pituitary is a gland the size of a pea that hangs under the hypothalamus on a short stalk. It makes growth hormone, and it makes hormones that tell other glands to work.
terms.example: The pituitary releases a hormone that travels in the blood to the thyroid gland and tells it to make more thyroid hormone.
terms.art: A pea-sized gland hanging on a thin stalk under the brain, resting in a small cup of bone.

terms.meaning: Growth hormone is a hormone from the pituitary gland. It makes bones grow longer and muscles grow bigger in children. It is released in bursts, and the biggest burst usually comes soon after deep sleep begins.
terms.example: Growth hormone tells the liver to make a second hormone. Together they make the cartilage cells in the growth plates divide.
terms.art: A sleeping girl with a small gland under her brain releasing a puff of dots, and a tiny arrow pointing to the end of a leg bone.

terms.meaning: A growth plate is a thin layer of cartilage near each end of a long bone in a child. Cartilage is the firm, bendy material in your ear. The bone gets longer here. At the end of the teenage years the plate turns to bone and growing in height stops.
terms.example: On an X-ray of a ten-year-old's hand, the growth plates show as dark gaps near the ends of the finger bones. A grown-up's hand has no gaps.
terms.art: An X-ray style drawing of a child's hand with thin dark gaps near the ends of the finger bones, beside a grown-up's hand with solid bones.

terms.meaning: The thyroid is a gland shaped like a butterfly at the front of the neck, below the voice box. Its hormone sets how fast cells use energy. A baby's brain and a child's bones need it to grow properly.
terms.example: A child whose thyroid makes too little hormone grows slowly and feels tired and cold. A daily tablet of the missing hormone puts this right.
terms.art: The front of a neck with a butterfly-shaped gland drawn below the bump of the voice box.

terms.meaning: Iodine is a chemical element. The thyroid gland cannot make its hormone without it, because each molecule of the hormone holds three or four iodine atoms. We get iodine from food and from iodised salt.
terms.example: The packet of salt in most Indian kitchens says 'iodised'. A tiny amount of an iodine compound has been added to it.
terms.art: A packet of iodised salt on a kitchen shelf beside a steel salt jar and a spoon.

terms.meaning: The pineal gland is a gland about the size of a grain of rice, deep in the middle of the brain. It makes melatonin when it is dark.
terms.example: In the evening, as the light fades, the body clock lets the pineal gland start making melatonin.
terms.art: A brain cut down the middle with a tiny gland the size of a rice grain coloured in near the centre, towards the back.

terms.meaning: Melatonin is the hormone the pineal gland releases at night. It tells every part of the body that it is dark outside. Bright light in the evening holds it back.
terms.example: In a child who sleeps at about nine, melatonin begins to rise in the early evening and is highest in the middle of the night.
terms.art: A night window with a crescent moon, and a sleeping child with small dots spreading from the middle of the head through the body.

terms.meaning: The body clock is a group of about 20,000 nerve cells in the hypothalamus that keeps time. It runs a cycle of roughly 24 hours by itself. Morning light sets it right each day. Scientists call a cycle of about a day a circadian rhythm.
terms.example: People who travel from Chennai to London feel sleepy at the wrong time for some days. Their body clock is still on Indian time.
terms.art: A small clock face drawn inside a brain, just above the place where the two nerves from the eyes cross.

terms.meaning: Sleep pressure is the need for sleep that builds up the longer you stay awake. It falls again while you sleep. It is separate from the body clock.
terms.example: After a long afternoon nap you are not sleepy at bedtime. The nap has taken away some of your sleep pressure.
terms.art: A tumbler slowly filling with water through the day, and emptying during the night.

terms.meaning: Cortisol is a hormone from the outer part of the adrenal glands. It rises in the last hours of the night and is highest soon after you wake. It helps release stored fuel for the day. It also rises during long-lasting stress.
terms.example: Your cortisol is rising before your alarm rings. Your body has started getting ready for the day while you are still asleep.
terms.art: A child asleep at dawn with pale light at the window and a rising line drawn above the bed.

terms.meaning: A steroid hormone is a hormone that the body makes from cholesterol, a fatty substance. It is small and fatty, so it can pass through the oily skin of a cell. Inside, it switches certain genes on or off.
terms.example: Cortisol and oestrogen are steroid hormones. Their effects come slowly and last for hours or days.
terms.art: A small ring-shaped molecule slipping through the skin of a cell and reaching a coil of DNA inside.

terms.meaning: Amplifying means making a small signal bigger. One hormone molecule on one receptor sets off a chain of steps inside the cell. Each step switches on many molecules of the next step.
terms.example: One adrenaline molecule on a liver cell can lead to the release of many thousands of glucose molecules.
terms.art: One dot touching a cell, then a widening fan of more and more dots inside the cell, ending in a crowd of dots leaving it.

terms.meaning: The half-life of a hormone is the time the body takes to clear half of it from the blood. A hormone with a short half-life gives a short message.
terms.example: Adrenaline has a half-life of only a few minutes. So a few minutes after a fright, most of it has gone.
terms.art: Four tumblers in a row holding 16, 8, 4 and 2 red beads, with a small clock between each.

terms.meaning: Puberty is the time when a child's body changes into a grown-up body. It begins when the hypothalamus tells the pituitary to wake the ovaries or the testes. They then make much more of their hormones.
terms.example: Puberty usually begins between 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys. It brings a few years of fast growth.
terms.art: A height chart on a wall with pencil marks close together for some years and then three marks far apart.

explanations.concept: The endocrine system: glands that release hormones into the blood
explanations.definition: The endocrine system is the set of glands and cells that make hormones. A hormone is a chemical that is released into the blood, travels round the body and changes what certain cells do.
explanations.description: Start at the top. The hypothalamus and the pituitary sit under the brain. The pineal gland is in the middle of the brain. The thyroid is at the front of the neck. The two adrenal glands sit on the kidneys. The pancreas lies behind the stomach, and small groups of its cells make insulin. Lower down are the ovaries in girls and the testes in boys. Why does the body need this system when it already has nerves? A nerve reaches only the cells it touches. Some jobs need a message to reach nearly every cell and to last for hours or years, such as growing. Blood already goes everywhere, so a chemical in the blood is a cheap way to tell the whole body one thing. This list of glands is a simplification. The stomach, the fat under your skin, the heart and the kidneys also release hormones. Scientists have named more than fifty human hormones, and they are still finding more.
examples: The thyroid gland, with its hormone that sets how fast cells use energy.
The adrenal glands, with adrenaline from the inner part and cortisol from the outer part.
The stomach, which is not called a gland but releases a hormone that makes you feel hungry.
explanations.art: A child's body outline, front view, with the hypothalamus and pituitary, pineal gland, thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas and ovaries marked in different colours, each joined by a thin line to its name.

explanations.concept: Adrenaline: the alarm that nerves start and a hormone carries on
explanations.definition: Adrenaline is a hormone released by the inner part of the adrenal glands during fright, excitement or hard exercise. It prepares the body for sudden effort.
explanations.description: When your brain judges that something is urgent, it signals a set of nerves called the sympathetic nerves. These nerves reach the heart, the skin and the gut directly, so the heart speeds up in about a second. The same nerves reach the inner part of the adrenal glands. Within seconds the glands release adrenaline into the blood. Adrenaline then does the same kind of work as those nerves, and it reaches cells that nerves do not touch. The heart beats faster and harder. The airways widen. The liver releases glucose, which is fuel. Blood is sent to the big muscles and away from the skin and the gut. All this is useful if you must run or fight. The American scientist Walter Cannon described it in 1915 and called it the 'fight or flight' response. Why does the thumping last after the danger has gone? A nerve signal stops in a moment. Adrenaline stays in the blood until the body has broken it down, and that takes a few minutes.
examples: A dog barks behind you. Your heart is pounding before you have turned round, and it is still pounding a minute later.
Before a race or a stage performance, your hands feel cold and your mouth feels dry. Blood has been moved away from the skin, and less saliva is being made.
In the Sitting-Still Alarm Test, most children's pulse rises during the timed sums, though no muscle is working hard.
explanations.art: A girl turning towards a barking dog, with a see-through view of her body showing nerves running from the spine to the heart and to the two adrenal glands, and small dots leaving the glands into the blood.

explanations.concept: One hormone, different answers: the receiving cell decides
explanations.definition: A hormone does not carry an instruction inside it. What happens depends on the receptor a cell has, and on what that cell is built to do.
explanations.description: Adrenaline makes heart muscle beat harder. The same adrenaline makes the muscle in the wall of the gut relax. It narrows the small blood vessels in the skin and widens those in the big muscles. How can one chemical do opposite things? In 1948 the American scientist Raymond Ahlquist proposed the answer. Cells carry different kinds of adrenaline receptor. He called them alpha and beta. Each kind starts a different chain of events inside the cell. So the meaning of the message is set by the receiver. Other hormones show the same thing. Thyroid hormone makes a child's bones grow, and the same hormone makes a tadpole's tail shrink away. Melatonin rises in the dark in humans, who then get sleepy. It also rises in the dark in rats and hamsters, who are active at night and are then wide awake. This is why calling melatonin 'the sleep hormone' is not quite right. It is a signal that says 'it is dark', and each kind of body answers in their own way.
examples: Adrenaline: heart muscle speeds up, gut muscle relaxes, liver cells release glucose.
Thyroid hormone: a child's leg bones lengthen, and a tadpole's tail is taken apart.
An asthma inhaler holds a medicine shaped to fit one kind of adrenaline receptor, the kind that opens the airways.
explanations.art: One small molecule drawn three times, arriving at a heart cell, a gut muscle cell and a liver cell, with a different arrow coming out of each cell.

explanations.concept: The chain of command: hypothalamus, pituitary and the glands below
explanations.definition: The hypothalamus releases hormones that tell the pituitary what to do. The pituitary releases hormones that tell other glands what to do. Those glands report back through the blood.
explanations.description: The hypothalamus is part of the brain, and it gets news from all over the body and from the senses. It sends tiny amounts of 'releasing hormones' down a short stalk to the pituitary. The pituitary answers by releasing its own hormones into the blood. One goes to the thyroid. One goes to the outer part of the adrenal glands. Two go to the ovaries or testes. One, growth hormone, goes to the liver, the bones and the muscles. Each step makes more hormone than the step before, so a very small signal from the brain becomes a large effect in the body. The pituitary is often called the 'master gland'. That is only partly right. It takes its orders from the hypothalamus. And when the thyroid has made enough hormone, that hormone itself tells the hypothalamus and the pituitary to ease off. So the orders run in a circle. Some glands are not in this chain at all. The adrenal glands release adrenaline on a signal from nerves, and the pancreas releases insulin when it senses sugar.
examples: Hypothalamus to pituitary to thyroid: three glands and three hormones, one after another.
When there is plenty of thyroid hormone in the blood, the pituitary sends less of its 'make more' hormone.
Adrenaline skips the chain. Nerves signal the adrenal glands directly, which is why it is so quick.
explanations.art: A diagram with the hypothalamus at the top, an arrow down to the pea-sized pituitary, arrows from the pituitary to the thyroid, an adrenal gland and a bone, and a dotted arrow curving back up from the thyroid to the hypothalamus.

explanations.definition: Children grow taller because cartilage cells in the growth plates of their bones divide, and bone then replaces the cartilage. Growth hormone and thyroid hormone keep this going. At the end of puberty the plates turn to bone and growth in height stops.
explanations.description: Between about four years old and puberty, most children grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year. The growing happens in the growth plates, thin layers of cartilage near the ends of the long bones. Growth hormone from the pituitary drives it. Growth hormone acts on the plates directly. It also tells the liver to release a second hormone, which makes the cartilage cells divide. Thyroid hormone is needed as well, and so are food and sleep. Growth hormone comes in bursts through the day and night. In 1968 Yasuro Takahashi and his colleagues sampled the blood of sleeping volunteers every 30 minutes. They found that the biggest burst begins when deep sleep begins. So 'you grow in your sleep' is partly true. It is also a simplification, because some growth hormone is released by day, and one late night does not make anyone shorter. In puberty, the ovaries and testes make far more of their hormones, and growth speeds up for a few years. Then one of those hormones, oestrogen, makes the growth plates turn to bone. Boys make oestrogen too, in smaller amounts, and it closes their growth plates as well.
examples: A girl who was 128 centimetres on her ninth birthday is about 134 centimetres on her tenth.
At the fastest point of puberty, girls grow about 8 centimetres in a year and boys about 9 and a half.
In 1994 doctors described a man of 28 whose body could not answer oestrogen. His growth plates had never closed, and he was still growing.
explanations.art: A leg bone of a child with a thin band of cartilage near each end, a zoomed-in circle showing stacked cartilage cells dividing, and a small pituitary gland above sending dots towards the bone and the liver.

explanations.concept: The thyroid: the pace of your cells, and why salt is iodised
explanations.definition: The thyroid gland makes a hormone that sets how fast cells use energy. Growth and brain development depend on it. The gland needs iodine to make the hormone.
explanations.description: Nearly every cell in your body is a target cell for thyroid hormone. With too little of it, cells work slowly. A child with too little grows slowly, feels cold and tired, and may find it hard to concentrate. A baby with too little, before or after birth, can be left with lasting harm to the brain. Each molecule of thyroid hormone holds iodine atoms, so no iodine means no hormone. A child of ten needs about 120 millionths of a gram of iodine a day. That is too small an amount to see. In many hill regions and river plains the soil holds little iodine, so the food grown there holds little too. The gland then swells as it tries harder, and the swelling in the neck is called a goitre. From 1956, the Indian doctor Vulimiri Ramalingaswami and his colleagues ran a long trial in the Kangra Valley of Himachal Pradesh. Villages that got salt with added iodine had far fewer goitres after some years. Villages that got plain salt did not change. India began a national goitre programme in 1962, and today nearly all salt sold for eating is iodised.
examples: The word 'iodised' on the salt packet in your kitchen.
Many hospitals test a drop of blood from a newborn baby's heel to check the baby's thyroid hormone, because early treatment protects the brain.
A tadpole with no thyroid hormone stays a tadpole and never becomes a frog.
explanations.art: A map-style drawing of a Himalayan valley with two villages, one receiving sacks marked 'iodised salt' and one receiving plain sacks, and a small drawing of a neck with a swollen thyroid beside it.

explanations.concept: How sleep is timed: a clock, light, melatonin and sleep pressure
explanations.definition: Two things together decide when you feel sleepy. One is the body clock, which sends out melatonin when it is dark. The other is sleep pressure, which builds up the longer you are awake.
explanations.description: The body clock is a small group of nerve cells in the hypothalamus. It keeps a cycle of about 24 hours by itself. In the evening it lets the pineal gland start making melatonin. Melatonin travels in the blood and tells every organ that night has come. It does not knock you out. It helps the body shift towards sleep, and it works together with sleep pressure. Sleep pressure is a separate thing. It rises through the day and falls during sleep. The Swiss scientist Alexander Borbély put the two together in 1982, and his picture is still used. How does the clock know it is evening? Special cells in the back of the eye measure brightness, and blue light affects them most. They are not the cells you see with. They report straight to the clock. Bright light in the evening tells the clock it is still day, and the pineal gland holds melatonin back. In 1980 Alfred Lewy's team showed this in people. Later studies found that young children's melatonin falls very strongly in bright evening light. Towards morning, cortisol rises and melatonin falls, and the body gets ready to wake.
examples: On a camping trip with no electric light, most people get sleepy earlier than at home.
After a flight from Chennai to London, the clock in the hypothalamus is still about five hours ahead for some days.
A late afternoon nap lowers sleep pressure, so bedtime sleepiness comes later, though melatonin rises at its usual time.
explanations.art: A side view of a head showing light entering the eye, an arrow from the back of the eye to a tiny clock in the hypothalamus, and a second arrow to the rice-sized pineal gland, with a moon outside the window.

explanations.concept: The clock runs by itself, and the spinning Earth made it
explanations.definition: The body clock keeps going with no light and no clock on the wall. Each of its cycles is close to one turn of the Earth.
explanations.description: In 1999 Charles Czeisler and his colleagues kept volunteers for weeks in rooms with no clues about the time. Their body clocks ran a cycle of 24 hours and 11 minutes on average. So the clock is very nearly right, and a little slow. Morning light corrects it each day. Where is the clock kept? Inside each clock cell, a few genes make proteins. The proteins build up and then switch their own genes off. The proteins break down, and the genes switch on again. One round takes about a day. Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young worked this out in fruit flies and received the Nobel Prize in 2017. The same kind of clock ticks in nearly all your cells, in the liver, the skin and the gut. The clock in the hypothalamus keeps them in step. Why do living beings have clocks at all? The Earth has turned once a day for billions of years. Light, warmth and danger have come and gone on that beat. Bodies that got ready ahead of time did better. Plants, fungi and some bacteria keep daily clocks too.
examples: A person in a cave with no watch still sleeps and wakes about once every 24 hours.
A touch-me-not plant kept in the dark still folds and opens their leaves roughly on time for a few days.
Your body temperature is lowest in the last hours of the night, whether you are asleep or awake.
explanations.art: The Earth half in sunlight and half in shadow, with a small sleeping child on the dark side and a waking child on the bright side, and a tiny loop of arrows drawn inside one cell.

explanations.concept: Tiny amounts, big effects: how a cell amplifies a hormone
explanations.definition: Hormones work at amounts far too small to taste or see. A cell answers because each receptor that is switched on starts a chain inside the cell, and each step of the chain is bigger than the last.
explanations.description: At night the melatonin in a child's blood is about one part in ten thousand million. That is less than a pinch of salt stirred into a hundred big water tankers. How can so little do anything? First, receptors fit their hormone closely, so they catch it even when it is rare. Second, the cell amplifies. Adrenaline does not enter a liver cell. It joins a receptor on the outside. The receptor then switches on helper proteins inside. Each helper starts the making of many small molecules called second messengers. These switch on enzymes, and each enzyme releases many glucose molecules. The American scientist Earl Sutherland found the second messenger in the 1950s and received the Nobel Prize in 1971. Hormones of a second kind work differently. Steroid hormones and thyroid hormone go inside the cell and switch genes on or off. That is slower, and the effect lasts much longer. Measuring such tiny amounts was impossible until 1959. Then the physicist Rosalyn Yalow and the doctor Solomon Berson, in New York, invented a method that can find a millionth of a millionth of a gram in a small sample of blood. Yalow received the Nobel Prize in 1977. Berson had died in 1972.
examples: In the Ten Times Weaker test, most tongues lose the taste of sugar by the second or third tumbler. A hormone receptor would still catch it at the tenth.
Adrenaline acts in seconds because it only has to switch on proteins that are already there.
Cortisol acts over hours because cells must read genes and build new proteins.
explanations.art: A cell with one molecule on a receptor outside, and inside it a chain of steps drawn as one dot, then ten dots, then a hundred dots, ending in a stream of sugar molecules leaving the cell.

explanations.concept: Puberty: the hormones that change a child's body
explanations.definition: Puberty begins when the hypothalamus starts sending bursts of a releasing hormone to the pituitary. The pituitary then signals the ovaries or the testes, and they make much more oestrogen or testosterone.
explanations.description: This chain of three is fully built in a baby. Then it goes quiet for the whole of childhood. Some time between 8 and 13 in girls, and between 9 and 14 in boys, the hypothalamus starts it up again. Oestrogen and testosterone are steroid hormones. They switch on genes in many kinds of cell, so over a few years the body grows fast, changes shape, grows new hair and becomes able to make babies. Both hormones are found in both girls and boys, in different amounts. What starts the hypothalamus up? In 2003 two research teams found families in which puberty never began, and traced it to one gene. The gene is for a receptor on the hypothalamus cells. The signal that fits it is called kisspeptin, and without it the chain stays quiet. But what tells the kisspeptin cells that the time has come is still not known. Body size, food and genes all play a part. The age at which puberty starts is different for every child, and a wide range is healthy.
examples: Two friends of the same age may start their fast growth two or three years apart, and both are healthy.
Girls usually have their fastest growth about two years earlier than boys.
The same hormone that speeds growth in puberty, oestrogen, also ends it by closing the growth plates.
explanations.art: Three children of the same age but different heights standing against a wall chart, with a small diagram above them of the hypothalamus, pituitary and a lower gland joined by arrows.

explanations.concept: When a gland makes too little, and how people replace the hormone
explanations.definition: If a gland makes too little of a hormone, the cells that depend on it do not get their message. Doctors can often measure the hormone in blood and give the missing hormone as medicine.
explanations.description: A child whose pituitary makes too little growth hormone grows much more slowly than other children. A child whose thyroid makes too little hormone grows slowly and feels tired. A child whose pancreas makes no insulin has type 1 diabetes. In each case the missing hormone can be given. Thyroid hormone is a small, tough molecule and survives the stomach, so it can be a tablet. Insulin and growth hormone are proteins. The stomach would digest them like food, so they must be injected. Insulin was first used in Toronto in January 1922, on a boy of 14 named Leonard Thompson. Frederick Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and John Macleod did the work. Only Banting and Macleod were given the Nobel Prize in 1923, and they shared their prize money with the other two. Most short children do not have a hormone problem. They have short parents, or they are growing on their own later timetable. A doctor checks by plotting heights on a growth chart over many months.
examples: A daily thyroid tablet for a child whose gland makes too little.
Insulin injections or an insulin pump for a child with type 1 diabetes.
A growth chart in a child's health record, with a height marked every six months.
explanations.art: A doctor and a girl looking together at a growth chart with a curved line of dots, with a measuring scale on the wall behind them.

explanations.concept: Hormones are older than glands: plants, insects and single cells
explanations.definition: Chemical messages between cells are found in nearly all living beings, including those with no blood and no glands.
explanations.description: Plants make hormones. One of them, ethylene, is a gas. A ripening banana gives off ethylene, and the gas makes the fruits nearby ripen too. That is why one ripe banana in a bag of raw mangoes hurries them along. Another plant hormone, auxin, gathers on the shaded side of a shoot and makes the cells there grow longer, so the shoot bends towards light. Insects grow by hormones as well. A caterpillar sheds their skin when one hormone rises. A second hormone keeps them a caterpillar. When the second one falls, the next change makes a pupa and then a butterfly. Even single cells signal with chemicals. Yeast cells release a chemical that other yeast cells answer before they join together. Some of our own hormone molecules are very old. Melatonin has been found in plants and in bacteria. One idea is that it began, billions of years ago, as a chemical that protected cells from damage, and only later became a night signal. That idea is not proven.
examples: Put a ripe banana in a paper bag with a raw banana or a raw mango, and the raw fruit ripens sooner.
A silkworm caterpillar moults four times as a caterpillar, each time on a hormone signal.
A money plant on a windowsill bends towards the light because auxin gathers on the shaded side.
explanations.art: A paper bag holding a ripe yellow banana and two green mangoes with faint wavy lines of gas between them, beside a caterpillar shedding skin and a plant shoot bending to a window.

explanations.concept: Does your pounding heart cause the fear, or does the fear cause the pounding heart?
explanations.description: Most people would say: I saw the dog, I felt afraid, and so my heart pounded. In 1884 the American thinker William James turned this round. He said the body changes first, and the feeling of fear is our sensing of those changes. Scientists have argued about it ever since. In 1962 Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer injected students with adrenaline without telling them what it would do. They reported that the students' feelings depended on what was going on around them. In 1979 Gary Marshall and Philip Zimbardo repeated the test and did not get the same result. So that famous experiment is in doubt. In the Sitting-Still Alarm Test you can ask yourself: when my pulse was up, did I feel nervous, excited or nothing much?
examples: Your heart pounds before a race and before a scary film. The body change is much the same, but you call one excitement and the other fear.
Some people feel their heart race after strong coffee and feel no emotion at all.

perspectives.explanation: The body changes come first. We feel afraid because we sense our heart pounding and our muscles tensing. Without the body changes there would be a thought of danger but no feeling.

The same body changes happen in fear, anger and excitement, and they are too slow. So the body cannot be what tells these feelings apart. The brain makes the feeling and the body alarm at the same time.

A feeling needs two things: a stirred-up body, and the mind's explanation of why. The same pounding heart can become fear or joy, depending on what you think is going on. Later tests did not all agree with theirs.

perspectives.who: Lisa Feldman Barrett and others today
perspectives.explanation: The brain is always predicting what the body will need and reading the body's signals. A feeling is the brain's best guess at what those signals mean right now, built from past experience.

explanations.art: A girl at the start line of a race and the same girl facing a growling dog, each with the same pounding heart drawn in her chest and a different thought bubble above.

explanations.concept: Do screens before bed harm sleep, and is the light to blame?
explanations.description: Bright evening light holds back melatonin. That is settled. Whether the light from a phone or tablet is bright enough to matter much is still argued over. In 2015 Anne-Marie Chang and her colleagues had 12 adults read for four hours before bed, on a bright tablet for some nights and from a printed book for others. On tablet nights their melatonin rose about an hour and a half later, and they took about ten minutes longer to fall asleep. Other scientists point out that four hours at full brightness is a lot. A phone screen is far dimmer than daylight. In everyday life, they say, screens cost sleep mainly because people stay up later, and because games and videos keep the mind busy. The Dim Evening Test in this lesson changes only the room light, so that you can see what light alone does for you.
examples: A child who watches a film until 10:30 has lost an hour of sleep, whatever the light did.
A dim, warm bedside lamp gives the eye far less blue light than a white tube light on the ceiling.

perspectives.who: Anne-Marie Chang, Charles Czeisler and colleagues (2015)
perspectives.explanation: Light from a screen in the evening delays the body clock, holds back melatonin and makes people less alert the next morning. They measured all three.

perspectives.who: Michael Gradisar and other sleep researchers
perspectives.explanation: The effect of screen light on falling asleep is small, a matter of minutes. What matters more is the time taken from sleep and how stirring the content is. Dimming the screen is less important than stopping on time.

explanations.art: Two bedrooms side by side at night: in one a child reads a paper book under a small warm lamp, and in the other a child's face is lit blue-white by a tablet.

agreed.text: Hormones are real chemicals in the blood, present in tiny amounts, and they act only on cells that have receptors for them.
agreed.evidence: Since 1959, the method of Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson has let scientists measure hormones in blood directly. Raymond Ahlquist's idea of different receptors, from 1948, led to medicines that fit one receptor and not another, and those medicines work.

agreed.text: The inner part of the adrenal glands releases adrenaline, which raises the heart rate and blood pressure.
agreed.evidence: In 1894 George Oliver and Edward Schäfer in London showed that an extract of adrenal gland sharply raised blood pressure. In 1900 Jokichi Takamine and his assistant Keizo Uenaka purified the active chemical as crystals. Uenaka did the key laboratory work and is rarely named.

agreed.text: Growth hormone is released in bursts, and the largest burst is tied to the start of deep sleep.
agreed.evidence: Yasuro Takahashi, David Kipnis and William Daughaday measured it in 1968 by taking blood every 30 minutes through the night. When they delayed sleep, the burst was delayed too.

agreed.text: The thyroid needs iodine, and adding iodine to salt prevents goitre.
agreed.evidence: In the Kangra Valley trial that began in 1956, goitre fell sharply in the zones given iodised salt and stayed the same in the zone given plain salt.

agreed.text: Bright light at night holds back melatonin in humans.
agreed.evidence: Alfred Lewy and his colleagues showed it in 1980 by measuring melatonin in volunteers who were woken at night and put in bright light. It has been repeated many times, in adults and in children.

agreed.text: The human body clock runs a cycle very close to 24 hours with no outside clues.
agreed.evidence: Charles Czeisler's team measured it in 1999 in 24 people kept away from all time clues. The average was 24 hours and 11 minutes.

agreed.text: Oestrogen closes the growth plates in both girls and boys.
agreed.evidence: In 1994 doctors reported a man of 28 whose cells had no working oestrogen receptor. He was 204 centimetres tall, his growth plates were still open and he was still growing.

challenging.context: This card is about a name you will find in many books: the pituitary as the 'master gland'.
challenging.claim: The pituitary is the master gland that controls all the other glands.
challenging.for: The pituitary does send hormones that drive the thyroid, the outer part of the adrenal glands, the ovaries and the testes.
challenging.against: The pituitary takes its orders from the hypothalamus. The glands it drives send their own hormones back to slow it down. And adrenaline, insulin and melatonin are released with no order from the pituitary at all.

challenging.context: This card is about whether melatonin is truly a 'sleep hormone'.
challenging.claim: Melatonin is the hormone that makes you sleep.
challenging.who: A common saying, and the label on some bottles
challenging.for: In humans melatonin rises about two hours before the usual bedtime, and sleepiness follows.
challenging.against: Rats and hamsters are active at night, and their melatonin rises at night too. So melatonin signals darkness, and each animal answers differently. In studies, melatonin tablets shift the body clock, but they make people fall asleep only a little sooner. Children should take them only if a doctor says so.

challenging.context: This card is about the saying that children grow in their sleep.
challenging.claim: Children grow only while they are asleep.
challenging.for: The biggest burst of growth hormone each day begins when deep sleep begins.
challenging.against: Smaller bursts come in the daytime as well. Growth depends on hormone levels over weeks and months, and on food and genes. The bone-building that growth hormone starts goes on all day.

challenging.context: This card is about what comes first when you are frightened: the feeling or the body's alarm.
challenging.claim: We do not tremble because we are afraid. We are afraid because we tremble.
challenging.for: The heart can speed up within a second, before a person has had time to think. People often say 'I only realised how scared I was when I saw my hands shaking.'
challenging.against: The body's alarm is much the same in fear, anger and excitement, so the body alone cannot tell the feelings apart. A key experiment in this area, from 1962, did not give the same result when others repeated it.

challenging.context: This card is about blue light from phones and tablets at bedtime.
challenging.claim: Blue light from screens is the main reason screens spoil sleep.
challenging.for: The eye cells that report to the body clock are most affected by blue light, and a 2015 study found later melatonin and slower sleep after four hours of tablet reading.
challenging.against: A screen is far dimmer than daylight, and the measured delay in falling asleep was about ten minutes. Many sleep scientists think later bedtimes and exciting content do more harm than the light does.

challenging.context: This card is about whether hormones belong only to animals with glands and blood.
challenging.for: The word was first used in 1905 for chemicals carried in the blood of animals.
challenging.against: Plants make hormones such as auxin and ethylene and carry them in sap or release them into the air. Fungi and single cells signal to each other with chemicals too.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what the tiny pineal gland in the middle of the brain is for? This card tells the true story, with two ideas that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1649 the French thinker René Descartes wrote that the pineal gland was the main seat of the soul. He chose it because it is single and sits in the middle of the brain. Later, many doctors decided the opposite. They said it was a leftover with no job. In 1917 two Americans, Carey McCord and Floyd Allen, fed ground-up cow pineal glands to tadpoles. The tadpoles' dark skin soon turned pale. So the gland held a powerful chemical. Aaron Lerner, a skin doctor at Yale University, hoped the chemical might treat skin diseases. His team worked through more than 250,000 cow pineal glands. In 1958 they isolated a few thousandths of a gram of it and named it melatonin. It did almost nothing to human skin. But other scientists soon found that animals make it in the dark. In 1980 Alfred Lewy's team showed that bright light at night switches off melatonin in people. The gland turned out to be the body's signal that night has come.
how_we_found_out.who: René Descartes, Carey McCord and Floyd Allen, Aaron Lerner and his team, and Alfred Lewy and his team
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: First, that the pineal gland is the seat of the soul. Later, that it is a useless leftover. The pale tadpoles showed that the gland makes a powerful chemical, and measurements in the dark and in the light showed that the chemical is a night signal.
how_we_found_out.art: A glass jar of dark tadpoles beside a second jar of pale tadpoles on a laboratory bench, with a tiny cone-shaped gland drawn above them.

big_questions.q: Adrenaline speeds up the heart and slows down the gut. So where is the meaning of a message kept: in the message or in the one who receives it?
big_questions.hint: Think of a school bell. What does it mean at 9 in the morning, and what does it mean at 3:30?

big_questions.q: Growing happens without your choosing, and so does feeling sleepy. How much of what your body does is decided by you?
big_questions.hint: Make two lists: things your body did today that you chose, and things your body did that you did not choose.

big_questions.q: In the Alarm Test your heart sped up for a sum on paper. Why would a body sound an alarm for something that cannot hurt it?
big_questions.hint: The alarm system is very old. What kinds of urgent thing did it meet long ago, and what kinds does it meet now?

big_questions.q: The body clock keeps time with the turning Earth. If people lived on Mars, where a day is 40 minutes longer, would their bodies ever fit in?
big_questions.hint: The human clock runs 11 minutes slow and is corrected by light each morning. How big a correction can it take?

big_questions.q: If a medicine could make every child grow 10 centimetres taller, should healthy children take it?
big_questions.hint: Who decides what the right height is? What might be lost, and who could not afford it?

big_questions.q: A banana ripens their neighbours with a gas, and your pineal gland tells your liver it is night. Is a hormone a kind of language?
big_questions.hint: What does a language need? A sender, a signal, a receiver who answers. Is anything missing?

story.title: What the Water Told Them
story.note: A made-up story. Girija, Suhas, Shanta Atte and the two rock pools are imagined. Dharwad is a real city in Karnataka. The science is real. Asian common toads lay strings of eggs in rain pools at the start of the monsoon. In 2017 Santosh Mogali, Srinivas Saidapur and Bhagyashri Shanbhag of Karnatak University in Dharwad reported that tadpoles of this toad, kept in water that was slowly lowered, became toadlets sooner and at a smaller size than tadpoles kept in steady water. The story stretches the difference a little, so that it is easy to see. The change from tadpole to toad is driven by thyroid hormone. Work on other species, by Robert Denver in the United States, showed that falling water raises a stress hormone in the tadpole, and that this pushes thyroid hormone up.
text: The first real rain of June came at night, and by morning the toads had been.

Behind the house, where the hill showed its bare rock, there were two hollows that held water after rain. They were the same size, each about as wide as a bullock-cart wheel and as deep as Girija's hand was long. In each one lay strings of black dots in clear jelly, looped round and round like a dropped necklace.
'That one is mine,' said Suhas, pointing to the hollow nearer the tamarind tree. He was seven and claimed things quickly.
'Then this one is mine,' said Girija. She was ten, and she had already begun to worry.

She had reason. Last year the rain had come like this, with one great night of water, and then it had stopped for eighteen days. The hollows had dried to a grey crust. She remembered what had been in the crust.
In four days the dots had tails. In a week the pools were full of tadpoles, each smaller than a grain of cooked rice, black and busy. They scraped at the green fuzz on the rock all day long.
The rain did not come back.

On the eighth morning Girija took a piece of chalk from her school bag and drew a line on the rock just at the edge of her water. By evening the water had drawn back from the line by the width of her thumb. So she took the small steel pot to the well, filled it, carried it up the slope and poured it in, slowly, down the side of the rock so that the tadpoles would not be knocked about. The water came back to the line.
'You have to fill yours too,' she told Suhas.
'Tomorrow,' said Suhas.
She filled hers every evening after that. Five pots, sometimes six. The rope of the well made a red mark across her palms. Her chalk line stayed wet.

Suhas filled his twice, and then there was a cricket match, and then he forgot. His water went down a thumb's width each day. A pale ring showed on the rock where it had been. Then a second ring inside the first.
'They will die,' Girija said. 'You know that. They will be stuck in the mud like last year.'
Suhas looked at his pool and looked unhappy, and went to play.

Their aunt came on Sunday. Shanta Atte worked at the university, in the building where the zoology people kept their tanks, and she knew how to keep four hundred tadpoles alive on boiled spinach. Girija took her up the slope and showed her both pools. She showed her the chalk line, and the steel pot, and her palms.
Atte crouched by Suhas's pool for a long time. It was hardly deeper than a finger now.
'Look at them,' she said. 'Not at the water. At them.'

Girija looked. Her brother's tadpoles looked different, and she needed a moment to see why. They had legs. Two thin back legs each, folded against the tail like a pair of bent pins. Some had the bumps of front legs under the skin.
She ran to her own pool. Her tadpoles were bigger than his. They were fat and glossy, and they had no legs at all, only two specks where legs might one day be.
'Mine are behind,' she said. It came out as a wail. 'I carried all that water and mine are behind!'
'Are they?' said Atte. She did not say anything else about it. She asked what was for lunch.

Nine days later Suhas's pool was a film of water over mud, and the mud was hopping. Toads no bigger than Girija's smallest fingernail, each a perfect toad, with a stub of tail still on some of them. They climbed the pale rings on the rock and went off into the grass under the tamarind. By evening there was only mud, and nothing was stuck in it.
Suhas was unbearable at dinner. 'Mine are finished. Mine are toads. Yours are still babies.'

Girija did not answer. She was thinking about the two pools. The eggs had come on the same night. The sun was the same, and the green fuzz on the rock was the same. Only one thing had been different, and she had carried it up the hill herself, five pots every evening.

She had thought the water was only the place where the tadpoles lived. But his tadpoles had known their pool was going. Nobody had told them. The water had told them, a thumb's width a day, and they had hurried. They had left early, and they had left small.
And hers? Every evening she had brought her pool back up to the chalk line. Every evening she had been telling them something too. There is time, she had been saying. Stay. Eat. Grow.
They were not behind. They had done exactly what she had told them.

The next evening she went up with the steel pot and stood at her pool for a while. Then she bent and rubbed out the chalk line with her thumb, and drew a new one a little lower down. She poured in two pots, only to the new line.
The evening after that, she drew it lower again.
On the sixth day there were legs.
Her toads left twelve days after her brother's. She put one on her palm beside a mark she had made on her finger for the size of his. Hers was clearly bigger.
'Mine were first,' said Suhas.
'Mine are bigger,' said Girija.
They looked at Atte, who was shelling peas and seemed not to have heard.
That night it rained on the hill, hard, for the first time in five weeks. In the morning both hollows were full to the brim, and there were new strings of black dots in each.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Girija thinks of the water as a home that she must keep safe. The turn comes when she sees that the water is also a message. A tadpole becomes a toad when thyroid hormone rises in their body. A tadpole senses that the pool is shrinking, and a stress hormone then pushes the thyroid hormone up early. So the change comes sooner, at a smaller size. Girija's tadpoles got no such signal, so they kept eating and growing. Neither set did anything wrong. Each tadpole timed the change by a hormone, and the hormone answered the news from outside. Children's bodies do the same when hormones time growth, sleep and puberty by food, light and the seasons.
ask: The two pools had the same eggs, the same sun and the same food. What was the one thing that differed?
Why might leaving the pool early and small be a good choice for a tadpole whose pool is drying?
Why might staying longer and leaving bigger be a good choice for a tadpole whose pool stays full?
Girija said her filling had been 'telling them something'. What do you think she meant?
What news from outside does your own body use to time things, such as feeling sleepy or feeling hungry?

games.title: Gland Trios: who releases what, and what does it do?
games.context: This is a card game about ten hormones. Each hormone has three cards: where it is made, its name and its job. You collect the three cards that belong together and read them aloud as one sentence.

printables.title: 30 trio cards to cut out
items: Gland: the inner part of the adrenal glands, on top of the kidneys.
Hormone: adrenaline.
Job: makes the heart beat faster and harder, widens the airways and makes the liver release glucose.
Gland: the outer part of the adrenal glands, on top of the kidneys.
Hormone: cortisol.
Job: rises before you wake and releases stored fuel for the day. It also rises in long-lasting stress.
Gland: the pituitary, the size of a pea, under the brain. This card is for its bone hormone.
Hormone: growth hormone.
Job: makes bones grow longer at the growth plates. The biggest burst comes when deep sleep begins.
Gland: the thyroid, shaped like a butterfly, at the front of the neck.
Hormone: thyroid hormone, which holds iodine atoms.
Job: sets how fast cells use energy. A child's bones and a baby's brain need it to grow.
Gland: the pineal gland, the size of a grain of rice, in the middle of the brain.
Hormone: melatonin.
Job: tells every part of the body that it is dark outside. Bright light holds it back.
Gland: small groups of cells in the pancreas, behind the stomach.
Hormone: insulin.
Job: after a meal, tells muscle, fat and liver cells to take glucose in from the blood.
Gland: the ovaries, low in the belly of a girl or woman.
Hormone: oestrogen.
Job: brings the body changes of puberty in girls. In girls and boys it closes the growth plates.
Gland: the testes of a boy or man.
Hormone: testosterone.
Job: brings the body changes of puberty in boys, such as a deeper voice and bigger muscles.
Gland: the hypothalamus, the size of an almond, a part of the brain.
Hormone: releasing hormones, sent down a short stalk.
Job: tell the pituitary gland when to release its own hormones.
Organ: the stomach, which is not called a gland but makes a hormone.
Hormone: ghrelin.
Job: rises before a meal and tells the brain that it is time to eat.

The Insulin trio. Gland: small groups of cells in the pancreas, behind the stomach. Hormone: insulin. Job: after a meal, tells muscle, fat and liver cells to take glucose in from the blood.

rules: For 2 to 4 players. Shuffle the 30 cards. Deal 6 cards each for 2 players, or 5 each for 3 or 4 players. Hold your cards so that only you can see them.
Put the other cards face down in a pile. Turn the top card face up beside the pile. This starts the throw-away pile.
On your turn, take one card: the top card of the face-down pile, or the top card of the throw-away pile.
If you now hold all three cards of one hormone, lay them down and read them as one sentence. For example: 'The pineal gland releases melatonin, which tells the body it is dark.'
Any player may say 'Check!' Then turn over the answer sheet. If the three cards do not belong together, pick them up again and miss your next turn.
End your turn by putting one card from your hand face up on the throw-away pile.
The game ends when the face-down pile is used up, or when one player has no cards left. The player with the most trios wins.
To play alone: shuffle the cards, start a timer and sort them into 10 trios. Check with the answer sheet. Play again and try to beat your time.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 30 cards. 2. Lay them face up and find one trio together as an example. 3. Shuffle and deal. 4. Make the two piles.
flow.say: Each hormone has three cards. One says where it is made, one gives its name and one gives its job. Let's find one trio together first.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Find one trio together. Then shuffle and deal.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gland Trios. Here you cut out the cards and learn what a trio is.
flow.parent: If many names are new, play the first game with all hands face up on the floor and help each other.

flow.say: Before you pick up, look at your hand. Which hormone are you closest to finishing? Which card is missing?
flow.kid: Pick up a card. Lay down a trio if you have one. Read it aloud. Throw one card away.
flow.context: This is the main part of Gland Trios. Here you collect trios and read each one as a sentence.

ask.q: Two trios start at the adrenal glands. How do you tell their cards apart?
good: One is the inner part, which makes adrenaline for an alarm.
The other is the outer part, which makes cortisol for waking and long stress.

flow.parent: Reading the trio aloud as one sentence is the learning step. Do not let it be skipped.

flow.do: 1. Count each player's trios. 2. Lay the Adrenaline trio beside the Melatonin trio. 3. Ask what the two hormones have in common and how they differ.
flow.say: Look at adrenaline and melatonin side by side. What is the same about how they travel? What is different about how long they last?
flow.kid: Count your trios. Put adrenaline beside melatonin. Say one thing the same and one thing different.
flow.context: This is the last step of Gland Trios. Here you compare two hormones.

check.q: Which trio is made by an organ that is not called a gland?
check.why: The stomach makes the hunger hormone, ghrelin. The stomach is not on the usual list of glands, yet it releases a hormone into the blood. Choosing another trio may mean thinking that only the named glands make hormones.

games.title: Clear the Alarm: how many rounds until the adrenaline has gone?
games.context: This is a game of chance about how a hormone fades from the blood. You start with 32 paper tokens that stand for adrenaline after a fright. Each round you shake them, and about half are removed. You guess how many rounds it will take to clear them, and then you find out.

printables.title: Tokens to make for each player
items: Cut 32 small squares of paper or thin card, each about as wide as your thumbnail.
Colour one side of every square red with a crayon or sketch pen. Leave the other side plain.
You can use 32 flat seeds or buttons with one side marked, if that is easier.

printables.title: Score sheet for one game
items: My guess: the alarm will be cleared in __ rounds.
Start: 32 tokens.
After round 1: __ tokens left.
After round 2: __ tokens left.
After round 3: __ tokens left.
After round 4: __ tokens left.
After round 5: __ tokens left.
After round 6: __ tokens left.
After round 7: __ tokens left.
After round 8: __ tokens left.
Cleared (2 tokens or fewer) after round __.

rules: Each player needs 32 tokens and a steel tumbler. The tumbler is the blood. The tokens are adrenaline molecules after a fright.
Before you start, every player writes a guess: after how many rounds will 2 tokens or fewer be left?
A round goes like this. Shake the tokens in the tumbler and tip them out on the floor. Every token that lands red side up has been broken down by the body. Take those away.
Count the tokens that are left and write the number on the score sheet. Put them back in the tumbler for the next round.
You are cleared when 2 tokens or fewer are left. Write down the round.
The player whose guess was closest to their own real number of rounds wins. Alone, play three games and see how close your guess gets.
Second game, 'Fright again': play as before, but after round 2 add 16 new tokens. That is a second fright. Guess first how many rounds it will take now.
