flow.do: 1. Make 32 tokens for each player. 2. Copy the score sheet. 3. Explain that each round, about half of the adrenaline is broken down. 4. Each player writes a guess.
flow.say: After a fright there is extra adrenaline in your blood. Your body breaks it down bit by bit. How many rounds do you think it takes to clear 32 tokens? Why?
flow.kid: Make your 32 tokens. Guess how many rounds will clear them. Write your guess and your reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clear the Alarm. Here you make the tokens and write your guess.
flow.parent: Many children guess 2 rounds, because half and half again sounds like all of it. Do not correct the guess.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds until 2 tokens or fewer are left. 2. Write the number left after every round. 3. Compare the real number of rounds with the guess.
flow.say: Shake, tip and take away the red ones. Count what is left each time. Watch how the numbers go down.
flow.kid: Shake and tip. Take away the red ones. Write the number left. Go on until 2 or fewer remain.
flow.context: This is the main part of Clear the Alarm. Here you play the rounds and write down what is left.

ask.q: The numbers went down fast at first and slowly at the end. Why?
good: Each round takes away about half of what is there.
Half of 32 is 16, but half of 4 is only 2.

flow.parent: Most games take 4 to 6 rounds. The numbers will not be exact halves, because each token lands by chance.

flow.do: 1. Play 'Fright again', adding 16 tokens after round 2. 2. Ask what the game shows about a real fright. 3. Read the parent note together.
flow.say: In a real body, each round would be a few minutes. What does this game tell you about why your heart keeps thumping after a fright is over?
flow.kid: Play again. Add 16 tokens after round 2. Say what the game shows about a real fright.
flow.context: This is the last step of Clear the Alarm. Here you add a second fright and say what the game shows.
flow.parent: After your child has answered: the time in which half of a hormone is cleared is called its half-life. For adrenaline in the blood it is a few minutes. So the hormone part of an alarm fades over several minutes and cannot stop at once. The game is a model. In a real body the nerves calm the heart as well.

check.q: A hormone is cleared by half every round. After 3 rounds, how much of it is left?
check.why: Half is left after one round, a quarter after two and one eighth after three. Choosing 'none' may mean taking away the same amount each round. The body takes away the same share each time, so the amount removed gets smaller.

experiments.title: The Sitting-Still Alarm Test: can pressure alone speed up your heart?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sit still on a chair the whole time. A helper counts your pulse while you rest, while you count slowly aloud, and while you race a timer on hard sums. Then the helper keeps counting for three more minutes. You will find out whether your body sounds an alarm when no muscle is working, and how long the alarm takes to fade.
experiments.question: If you sit still and race a timer on hard sums, does your pulse change? If it does, how many minutes does it take to come back to your resting pulse?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you race the timer, will your pulse go up, go down or stay the same? If you think it will change, guess how long it will take to come back. Write both guesses, and write the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: calm or pressure. In both tasks you sit on the same chair, keep your body still and speak aloud for one minute. That way, talking and sitting are the same in both, and only the pressure differs. The same helper counts the pulse at the same wrist for 30 seconds each time. Rest for 3 minutes before the first count. Do not run about, and do not drink tea, coffee or cola, in the hour before. Do the pressure task twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a chair with a back, and a table to rest your arm on
a clock, watch or phone timer that shows seconds
a helper to count your pulse
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: This is a game, and nobody should be frightened or scolded in it. If your child becomes upset, stop and try another day. Never test an alarm by startling someone. Feel the pulse at the wrist only, never at the neck.

schedule.what: Practise finding the pulse. Count it at rest, during calm counting, during two timed pressure tasks and for three minutes afterwards. Draw a line graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with every count. Multiply each 30-second count by 2 to get beats a minute. Draw a line graph with the times along the bottom and beats a minute up the side. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: pulse before, during and after racing the timer
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A girl sitting on a chair with her forearm resting on a table, palm up, and her mother's two fingertips pressed lightly on the inside of the girl's wrist below the thumb, with a phone timer on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still. A helper finds your pulse at the wrist and counts it for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The same girl counting aloud with a calm face while her mother keeps two fingers on her wrist and watches the timer.
setup.caption: 2. Count slowly aloud from 1 for one minute. The helper counts your pulse in the last 30 seconds.

setup.art: The same girl leaning forward a little with a frown of concentration, counting backwards fast, while the timer shows the seconds running down and her mother counts her pulse.
setup.caption: 3. Race the timer: count backwards from 200 in threes for one minute. The helper counts again.

setup.art: The girl sitting quietly with eyes resting on the table while her mother counts her pulse once more, and a notebook beside them shows a column of numbers.
setup.caption: 4. Sit quietly. The helper counts straight after, and at 1, 2 and 3 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Rest your child's forearm on the table, palm up. 2. Press two fingertips lightly on the wrist, below the thumb. 3. Count the beats for 30 seconds. 4. Let your child find their own pulse too.
flow.say: The pulse is the push of blood each time your heart beats. Let's practise counting it for 30 seconds.
flow.kid: Rest your arm on the table. Your helper finds your pulse. Count the beats for 30 seconds together.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test. Here you practise finding and counting the pulse.
flow.parent: Use two fingers, not the thumb, because the thumb has a pulse of its own. If you lose count, start the 30 seconds again.

flow.do: 1. Explain the plan: rest, then calm counting, then racing a timer on sums. 2. Ask what the pulse will do in the race. 3. Ask how long it will take to come back. 4. Write down both guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: You will sit still the whole time. When you race the timer, what will your pulse do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what your pulse will do in the race. Guess how long it takes to come back. Say why. Write it down.
flow.context: This step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test is for guessing. You guess before any pulse is counted.

good: It will stay the same, because I am not moving.
It will go up, because I feel my heart thump when I am nervous.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Both of these reasons are sensible.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits quietly for 3 minutes without talking. 2. Count the pulse for 30 seconds. 3. Wait half a minute and count again. 4. Ask whether the palms are dry or damp, and whether the mouth is wet or dry.
flow.say: Sit quietly and breathe normally. I will count your resting pulse twice.
flow.kid: Sit quietly for 3 minutes. Your helper counts your pulse twice. Notice your palms and your mouth.
flow.context: This step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test finds your resting pulse. Every later count is compared with it.
flow.parent: If the two counts differ by more than 3 beats, wait another minute and count a third time. Use the two that are closest.

flow.do: 1. Start a one-minute timer. 2. Your child counts aloud from 1, slowly, about one number each second. 3. Count the pulse during the last 30 seconds. 4. Write it down.
flow.say: Count aloud from 1, nice and slowly. There is no hurry and nothing to get wrong.
flow.kid: Count aloud from 1, slowly, for one minute. Your helper counts your pulse.
flow.context: This step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test is the calm task. It shows what talking by itself does to your pulse.

flow.do: 1. Start a one-minute timer. 2. Your child counts backwards from 200 in threes, aloud, as fast as possible. 3. Count the pulse during the last 30 seconds. 4. When the timer rings, your child sits silent. 5. Count for 30 seconds straight away, and again at 1, 2 and 3 minutes. 6. Ask about palms and mouth.
flow.say: Now race the timer. Count backwards from 200 in threes. Try to get below 140 before it rings. Go!
flow.kid: Count backwards from 200 in threes, fast. Try to pass 140. Then sit silent while your helper counts.
flow.context: This step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test is the pressure task. Here you race a timer, and then the helper follows your pulse for three minutes.
flow.parent: Keep your fingers on the wrist throughout. Do not correct mistakes in the sums. The pressure should come from the timer, not from you. For a child who finds threes easy, use sevens.

flow.do: 1. Check that the pulse is back near the resting count. 2. Repeat the race with a new task: count backwards from 300 in fours. 3. Count the pulse during the last 30 seconds. 4. Write it down.
flow.say: One try can be a fluke, so we race once more with a new sum. Ready? Go!
flow.kid: Race the timer once more. Count backwards from 300 in fours. Your helper counts your pulse.
flow.context: This step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test repeats the pressure task, so that you can see whether the result happens twice.
flow.parent: The second rise is often smaller than the first, because the task is no longer new. That is worth noticing and writing down.

flow.do: 1. Multiply every 30-second count by 2. 2. Mark each one on a line graph in the order it was taken. 3. Join the marks.
flow.say: Let's turn every count into beats a minute and put them on a graph.
flow.kid: Multiply each count by 2. Mark each one on a graph. Join the marks with a line.
flow.context: This step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test turns your counts into beats a minute and a line graph.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child claims, what they saw and why they think it happened. 2. Ask what else changed besides the pulse. 3. Only then read the parent note together. 4. Write three sentences in the notebook.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. What did your pulse do, and what did your palms and mouth do?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened. Write three sentences.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Sitting-Still Alarm Test. Here you say and write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

ask.q: No muscle was working hard. So what told your heart to speed up?
good: My brain decided the race was urgent and sent a signal.
Nerves to the heart, and adrenaline from the adrenal glands.

ask.q: Your heart sped up, but did your mouth make more saliva or less?
good: Less. It felt drier.
So the same alarm made one part do more and another part do less.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: in most children the pulse rises by 5 to 20 beats a minute in the race and is back near resting within 1 to 3 minutes. The brain judged the task urgent and signalled the sympathetic nerves. They speed the heart within a second or so, and they also signal the adrenal glands to release adrenaline. Be honest about the limit of this test. It cannot show how much of the rise was nerves and how much was adrenaline. Studies that sampled blood during mental sums found that adrenaline about doubles, which is still a small amount. So here the nerves probably did most of the work. In a real fright or a hard run, far more adrenaline is released. If the pulse did not rise at all, that is a real result too. Some children stay calm in this task.

check.q: Your pulse rose while you sat still and raced the timer. What does that show?
options: Sums use a lot of muscle
Talking always speeds the heart a lot
The body can sound an alarm from a thought alone
check.why: Nothing chased you and no big muscle worked. Your brain judged the race urgent, and signals went out to your heart. The calm counting shows that talking alone changes the pulse very little. Choosing 'talking' may mean forgetting what the calm task was for.

experiments.title: The Dim Evening Test: does evening light change when you get sleepy?
experiments.context: In this experiment you spend six evenings in two ways. On three evenings the room lights stay bright until bedtime. On three evenings you use only one small, dim lamp for the last hour and a half. Everything else stays the same. You will find out whether evening light changes how sleepy you feel and how soon you fall asleep.
experiments.question: If the lights are dim for the last hour and a half before bed, do you get sleepy sooner and fall asleep faster than on a bright evening?
experiments.predict: Guess first. On dim evenings, will you feel more sleepy, less sleepy or the same at bedtime? Will you fall asleep sooner, later or in the same time? Write your guess, and write the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the light. On all six evenings, eat dinner at the same time and switch the lights off for sleep at the same time. On all six evenings, use no phone, tablet or television in the last hour and a half. Do the same quiet things: read a paper book, draw, play a board game or talk. Take no nap in the day, and no tea, coffee or cola after 4 in the afternoon. Take turns: bright, dim, bright, dim, bright, dim. That way, a tiring day is as likely to fall on one kind of evening as on the other.
results_table: Sleepiness score 15 minutes before lights-off (1 to 5)
Next morning: how easy was waking? (1 to 5)

materials.item: a small lamp for dim evenings: a bedside lamp, a zero-watt night bulb, or a torch pointed at the ceiling
the usual ceiling lights of the room, for bright evenings
a clock
a paper book, drawing things or a board game
a notebook and pencil kept beside the bed
a grown-up to note the first yawn and to check quietly when you fall asleep

experiments.safety: On dim evenings, keep enough light to walk about safely. Do not cover a hot bulb with cloth or paper. The grown-up checks on the child quietly and does not wake them.

schedule.what: Plan the six evenings and write your guess. Evening 1 is bright. Fill in the first row.
Morning: write how easy waking was. Evening 2 is dim. Fill in the row.
Morning score. Evening 3 is bright. Fill in the row.
Morning score. Evening 4 is dim. Fill in the row.
Morning score. Evening 5 is bright. Fill in the row.
Morning score. Evening 6 is dim. Fill in the row.
Last morning score. Find the mean for bright evenings and for dim evenings. Draw a bar chart. Write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table each evening and add the morning score the next day. On day 7, find the mean sleepiness score and the mean minutes to fall asleep for the three bright evenings and for the three dim evenings. Draw two bars for each. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: mean minutes to fall asleep
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different, and the two bars may come out the same.

setup.art: A living room in the evening with a bright white tube light on the ceiling, and a girl and her father playing a board game on the floor with a wall clock showing half past seven.
setup.caption: 1. Bright evening: keep the usual room lights on until lights-off. No screens.

setup.art: The same room on another evening with the ceiling light off and one small warm lamp in a corner, the girl and her father playing the same board game in soft light.
setup.caption: 2. Dim evening: for the last hour and a half, use only one small lamp. No screens.

setup.art: A girl in bed writing a number in a notebook by her pillow, with a scale of five small faces from wide awake to eyes closing drawn at the top of the page.
setup.caption: 3. Fifteen minutes before lights-off, give yourself a sleepiness score from 1 to 5.

setup.art: A mother standing quietly at a bedroom door at night looking at a sleeping child, holding a small notebook, with a clock on the wall.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up looks in every 5 minutes and writes down when you are asleep.

flow.do: 1. Agree on one dinner time and one lights-off time for all six evenings. 2. Explain the two kinds of evening. 3. Ask for a guess and the reason. 4. Write the guess in the notebook.
flow.say: For six evenings only the light will change. Will dim light make a difference to your sleepiness? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Plan your six evenings. Guess what dim light will do. Say why. Write your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dim Evening Test. Here you plan six evenings and write your guess.

good: Dim light is like sunset, so my body may think it is night.
It will make no difference, because I get sleepy when I am tired.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Choose a lights-off time you can truly keep for six evenings.

flow.do: 1. Draw the table with six rows. 2. Write 'bright' or 'dim' against each evening, taking turns. 3. Draw the sleepiness scale: 1 is wide awake, 3 is a little sleepy, 5 is eyes closing. 4. Choose the dim lamp and try it.
flow.say: Let's draw the table and the sleepiness scale. Then we will try the dim lamp to check that we can still see.
flow.kid: Draw the table. Mark each evening bright or dim. Draw the sleepiness scale from 1 to 5.
flow.context: This step of the Dim Evening Test sets up the table, the sleepiness scale and the dim lamp.
flow.parent: A good dim lamp lets you read large print but makes small print hard. Put it low and behind the child, not at eye level.

flow.do: 1. An hour and a half before lights-off, set the light as planned and put screens away. 2. Note the time of the first yawn. 3. Fifteen minutes before lights-off, ask for the sleepiness score. 4. After lights-off, look in every 5 minutes and note when your child is asleep.
flow.say: It is time to set the light for this evening. Tell me your sleepiness score when I ask, from 1 to 5.
flow.kid: Set the light for this evening. Put screens away. Give your sleepiness score when asked.
flow.context: This step of the Dim Evening Test is done on each of the six evenings. Here you set the light and fill in one row.
flow.wait: Do this step on each of the six evenings.
flow.parent: To check for sleep, whisper your child's name once from the door. No answer and slow, even breathing counts as asleep.

flow.do: 1. On waking, ask how easy it was to wake up, from 1 to 5. 2. Write the score in last evening's row.
flow.say: How easy was it to wake up this morning? 1 is very hard and 5 is very easy.
flow.kid: When you wake, score how easy it was. 1 is very hard. 5 is very easy.
flow.context: This step of the Dim Evening Test is done each morning. Here you score how easy it was to wake up.
flow.wait: Do this step on the morning after each evening.

flow.do: 1. Add the three bright scores and divide by 3. 2. Do the same for the three dim scores. 3. Do the same for minutes to fall asleep. 4. Draw the bars. 5. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning. 6. Then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. Did the light make a difference for you? How sure are you?
flow.kid: Find the mean for bright and for dim evenings. Draw the bars. Say what you found and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Dim Evening Test. Here you find the means, draw a chart and say what the test shows.

ask.q: You knew which evenings were dim. Could that have changed your scores?
good: Yes. I expected to be sleepy, so I may have scored higher.
The minutes to fall asleep are fairer, because someone else measured them.

ask.q: Three evenings of each kind is a small number. What would make you more sure?
good: More evenings of each kind.
Other children doing the same test and getting the same result.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: special cells in the eye report brightness to the body clock. Bright evening light tells the clock it is still day, and the pineal gland holds back melatonin. In dim light, melatonin rises on time. Many families find more sleepiness and quicker sleep on dim evenings, but not all do. Three evenings of each kind is few, and one late party or one exciting day can swamp the effect. If your bars are equal, say so. That is an honest result.

check.q: Why were screens put away on bright evenings as well as on dim ones?
options: So that only the room light differed
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If screens were used on bright evenings only, you could not tell whether the room light or the screen made the difference. Choosing 'always harmful' may mean answering from a rule and not from the plan of the test.

experiments.title: Ten Times Weaker: how little sugar can your tongue still find?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make sugar water, and then make it ten times weaker, three times over. A helper mixes up the tumblers and you taste them without knowing which is which. You will find the weakest sugar water your tongue can pick up. Then you compare your tongue with a hormone receptor.
experiments.question: Each tumbler has ten times less sugar than the one before. Which is the last tumbler that still tastes sweet to you?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which will be the last tumbler you can taste as sweet: tumbler 1, 2, 3 or 4? Write your guess, and write the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the amount of sugar. Use the same drinking water, the same kind of tumbler and the same amount in each. Rinse the spoon before each transfer, so that no extra sugar is carried over. Taste without seeing the labels, because knowing the answer changes what people taste. Include one tumbler of plain water to catch guessing. Rinse your mouth with plain water between tastes. Do the whole tasting twice.

materials.item: steel or glass tumblers, all the same size
a tablespoon and a teaspoon
sugar
drinking water, about 1 litre
small slips of paper numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and W, and a pencil
a helper to shuffle the tumblers

schedule.what: Make four tumblers of sugar water, each ten times weaker than the last, and one of plain water. Taste them twice without seeing the labels. Find the last one you can taste.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for both rounds. Circle the weakest tumbler that you called sweet in both rounds. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think tumbler 4 has sugar in it though you cannot taste it.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: in how many of 2 rounds was each tumbler called sweet?
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Five identical steel tumblers in a row on a kitchen counter, each standing on a small slip of paper, with a jar of sugar, a tablespoon and a teaspoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Tumbler 1: stir 4 level teaspoons of sugar into 10 tablespoons of water.

setup.art: A hand moving one tablespoon of liquid from the first tumbler to the second tumbler, which already holds water.
setup.caption: 2. Tumbler 2: put 1 tablespoon from tumbler 1 into 9 tablespoons of water. Do the same from 2 to 3, and from 3 to 4.

setup.art: A girl with her back turned while her aunt slides the five tumblers into a new order, the paper slips hidden underneath them.
setup.caption: 3. A helper hides the labels and shuffles the tumblers.

setup.art: The girl tasting from a teaspoon with her eyes thoughtful, the five tumblers in front of her and a glass of plain water for rinsing.
setup.caption: 4. Taste a teaspoon from each. Say 'sweet' or 'not sweet'. Rinse your mouth between tastes.

flow.do: 1. Put 10 tablespoons of water in tumbler 1 and stir in 4 level teaspoons of sugar. 2. Put 9 tablespoons of water in tumblers 2, 3 and 4. 3. Move 1 tablespoon from tumbler 1 to tumbler 2 and stir. 4. Rinse the spoon. 5. Move 1 tablespoon from 2 to 3, then from 3 to 4, rinsing each time. 6. Put 10 tablespoons of plain water in tumbler W.
flow.say: Each tumbler will have ten times less sugar than the one before it. We rinse the spoon each time so that no extra sugar sneaks across.
flow.kid: Make tumbler 1 with sugar. Move one spoon from each tumbler to the next. Rinse the spoon each time.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Times Weaker. Here you make four tumblers of sugar water, each ten times weaker than the last.
flow.parent: Tumbler 1 is about one part sugar in ten, like a very sweet sherbet. Tumbler 2 is one part in a hundred. Tumbler 3 is one in a thousand. Tumbler 4 is one in ten thousand.

flow.do: 1. Stand each tumbler on its paper slip. 2. Ask which tumbler will be the last to taste sweet. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Which will be the last tumbler that you can still taste as sweet? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the last tumbler that will taste sweet. Say why. Write it down.
flow.context: This step of Ten Times Weaker is for guessing. You guess before you taste anything.

good: Tumbler 4, because there is still some sugar in it.
Tumbler 2, because after that there is too little to notice.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns away. 2. Slide the tumblers into a new order, keeping each on its slip. 3. Your child tastes one teaspoon from each and says 'sweet' or 'not sweet'. 4. Your child rinses with plain water between tastes. 5. Write the answers down, then shuffle and repeat.
flow.say: Taste each one and tell me: sweet, or not sweet? Rinse your mouth before the next. You will not know which is which.
flow.kid: Turn away while the tumblers are shuffled. Taste each one. Say sweet or not sweet. Rinse between tastes.
flow.context: This step of Ten Times Weaker is the tasting. Here you taste all five tumblers twice without seeing the labels.
flow.parent: Give a clean teaspoon, or rinse it, for every taste. If your child calls the plain water sweet, they are guessing. Do one more round.

flow.do: 1. Lift the tumblers to show the slips. 2. Circle the weakest tumbler called sweet in both rounds. 3. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning. 4. Ask whether tumbler 4 has sugar in it. 5. Only then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. Which was the last one you could taste? Is there sugar in tumbler 4?
flow.kid: Look at the labels. Circle the last tumbler you tasted as sweet. Say what you found and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ten Times Weaker. Here you find your weakest sweet tumbler and compare your tongue with a hormone receptor.

ask.q: You cannot taste tumbler 4. How do you know there is sugar in it?
good: I put it there myself, one spoon from tumbler 3.
Not tasting something does not mean it is absent.

ask.q: If you kept going, which tumbler would be as weak as melatonin in your blood at night?
good: About tumbler 10.
Six more tumblers after tumbler 4.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: most children taste tumbler 2 and lose the sugar at tumbler 3. Some lose it at tumbler 2. Your tongue finds sugar with receptors on taste cells. They belong to the same large family of receptors as the ones that catch adrenaline. But hormone receptors hold their hormone far more tightly. At night, melatonin in the blood is about one part in ten thousand million. That would be tumbler 10 in your row. Cells still answer it, because their receptors catch it and the cell then amplifies the signal.

check.q: Tumbler 4 tastes like plain water. What is the best thing to say about it?
options: It has sugar, but too little for my tongue
It has no sugar in it
The sugar has turned into water
check.why: You put sugar in, and sugar does not vanish when it is diluted. Your tongue's receptors need more of it before they answer. Choosing 'no sugar' may mean trusting the senses over what you know you did.

activities.title: Where Did You Feel It? A body map of one fright
activities.context: In this activity you remember a fright you really had, and mark on a drawing of a body every place where you felt something change. Someone else in the family does the same. You will notice how many far-apart parts answered one small event.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper
a pencil and a red crayon or sketch pen

activities.record: Keep both body maps. Under yours, write the number of places you marked and how long the feeling lasted. Write one question you want answered.

setup.art: A simple outline of a child's body drawn in pencil on a sheet of paper, with a red crayon beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a simple outline of a body, from head to feet.

setup.art: The same outline with red crosses on the chest, the tummy, both palms, the mouth and the knees, and a small word written beside each cross.
setup.caption: 2. Remember a real fright. Put a red cross on every place where you felt a change, and write a word beside it.

setup.art: A girl and her grandmother holding their two body maps side by side and pointing at crosses that are in the same places.
setup.caption: 3. Ask someone else to make their own map. Compare the two.

flow.do: 1. Each of you draws a body outline. 2. Each remembers one real fright, such as a loud bang or a near fall. 3. Mark a red cross wherever you felt a change. 4. Write one word beside each cross.
flow.say: Think of a time you got a real fright. Where in your body did you feel it? Mark every place, and give each one a word.
flow.kid: Draw a body. Remember a real fright. Mark each place you felt it. Write a word beside each cross.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Did You Feel It. Here you mark on a drawing where a fright showed up in your body.
flow.parent: Useful words are thump, tight, cold, dry, shaky, wobbly and fluttery. Do your own map without looking at your child's.

flow.do: 1. Put the two maps side by side. 2. Count the crosses on each. 3. Find the places that are marked on both.
flow.say: Let's compare. Which places did we both mark? Which did only one of us mark?
flow.kid: Put the maps side by side. Count the crosses. Find the places you both marked.
flow.context: This step of Where Did You Feel It compares two people's maps.

ask.q: What do you notice when you look at both maps?
good: We both marked the chest and the hands.
One fright changed lots of places that are far apart.

flow.do: 1. Ask how long the fright itself lasted. 2. Ask how long the feelings in the body lasted. 3. Ask how the news could reach so many places. 4. Write down one question to answer in this lesson.
flow.say: The bang lasted one second. How long did your body go on feeling it? How do you think the news got to all those places?
flow.kid: Say how long the fright lasted. Say how long your body felt it. Write one question you have.
flow.context: This is the last step of Where Did You Feel It. Here you ask how one event reached so many parts, and why it lasted.
flow.think: The danger was over in a second. Why would a body keep its alarm going for a minute or more?
flow.parent: Do not explain yet. The Sitting-Still Alarm Test and the cards that follow answer these questions.

activities.title: Gland Map: lay out the endocrine system at about its real size
activities.context: In this activity you draw round your own upper body and place a real object, or a paper shape, where each hormone gland sits. You will see how small the glands are and how far apart, and you will learn which hormone each one makes.

materials.item: old newspaper sheets taped together, big enough to lie on from head to hips
a sketch pen and sticky tape
an almond or a groundnut, for the hypothalamus
a dried pea or a chana, for the pituitary
a grain of rice, for the pineal gland
plain paper and scissors, to cut the larger glands
small slips of paper for labels

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors if needed.
activities.record: When the map is finished, take a photo or copy it small into your notebook, with each gland and its hormone labelled.

setup.art: A girl lying on her back on taped-together newspaper sheets while her mother draws round her head, shoulders and body down to the hips with a sketch pen.
setup.caption: 1. Lie on the newspaper. A helper draws round you from head to hips.

setup.art: The newspaper outline with an almond, a dried pea and a grain of rice placed inside the head, a paper butterfly on the neck, two small paper triangles and a paper leaf shape in the belly, and two small paper ovals near the hips.
setup.caption: 2. Place each gland: almond, pea and rice grain in the head, and paper shapes below.

setup.art: The same outline with two small paper labels beside each gland, one naming the gland and one naming its hormone.
setup.caption: 3. Label each gland with its name and its hormone.

flow.do: 1. Tape newspaper sheets together. 2. Your child lies on them and you draw round the head and body down to the hips. 3. Cut paper shapes: a butterfly 4 centimetres wide, two triangles 3 centimetres long, a leaf shape 10 centimetres long and two ovals 2 centimetres long.
flow.say: First we need an outline of you. Then we will cut the bigger glands out of paper.
flow.kid: Lie on the newspaper. Your helper draws round you. Then cut out the paper glands.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gland Map. Here you make your outline and cut the paper glands.
flow.parent: The sizes are rough guides for a child of about ten. The butterfly is the thyroid, the triangles are the adrenal glands, the leaf shape is the pancreas and the ovals are the ovaries or testes.

flow.do: 1. Before placing anything, ask where your child thinks each gland goes. 2. Place the almond low in the middle of the head, with the pea just under it. 3. Place the rice grain behind them, in the middle of the head. 4. Place the butterfly on the front of the neck. 5. Place the triangles on the back of the belly, a hand's width above the waist, and the leaf shape between them. 6. Place the ovals low near the hips.
flow.say: Where do you think each one goes? Put them where you think, and then we will check with the picture.
flow.kid: Guess where each gland goes. Place them. Then check with the picture and move any that are wrong.
flow.context: This step of Gland Map places each gland where it sits in the body.

ask.q: What surprises you about the sizes?
good: The pituitary is only a pea, and it sends out growth hormone for the whole body.
The pineal gland is a grain of rice.

flow.parent: Ovaries are inside the lower belly. Testes hang outside the body, below it. Use the correct names plainly.

flow.do: 1. Write each gland's name on one slip and its hormone on another. 2. Lay the slips beside the glands. 3. Mix up the slips and ask your child to put them back. 4. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Now the labels. Each gland gets its name and one hormone. Then I will mix them up for you.
flow.kid: Write a name label and a hormone label for each gland. Mix them up. Put them back.
flow.context: This is the last step of Gland Map. Here you label each gland with its name and one hormone.
flow.parent: The pairs are: hypothalamus and releasing hormones, pituitary and growth hormone, pineal and melatonin, thyroid and thyroid hormone, adrenal glands and adrenaline, pancreas and insulin, ovaries and oestrogen, testes and testosterone.

check.q: The glands are far apart and no wire joins them. How do their hormones reach the rest of the body?
options: Through the air in the lungs
check.why: Each gland is full of tiny blood vessels. The hormone passes into the blood, and the blood carries it everywhere within about a minute. Choosing another answer may mean picturing a gland as joined to one place, the way a nerve is.

activities.title: The Ripe Banana Test: a hormone that travels through the air
activities.context: In this activity you put raw green bananas into two paper bags. One bag also gets a ripe yellow banana. You look each day for four days. You will see a plant hormone at work, and you will see that a hormone does not need blood to travel.

materials.item: raw green bananas from the same bunch, as alike as possible
a ripe yellow banana with a few brown spots
paper bags or newspaper wraps, the same size
a pencil and a notebook

schedule.what: Guess what will happen. Put two green bananas in each bag and add the ripe banana to one bag. Fold both bags shut and keep them side by side.
Open both bags, look at the green bananas and write down their colour. Close the bags again.
Look again and write down the colour.
Look for the last time. Compare the two bags and say what happened and why. Then eat the bananas.

activities.record: Each day, give the green bananas in each bag a colour score: 1 for all green, 2 for green with some yellow, 3 for mostly yellow, 4 for all yellow. Write both scores in a small table.

setup.art: Four green bananas and one ripe spotted yellow banana on a kitchen counter beside two brown paper bags.
setup.caption: 1. Put two green bananas in each bag. Add the ripe banana to one bag only.

setup.art: Two folded paper bags side by side on a shelf, one marked with a pencilled letter R.
setup.caption: 2. Fold both bags shut. Mark the one with the ripe banana. Keep them side by side.

setup.art: A girl looking into both open bags on the third day, one holding yellowing bananas and the other holding bananas that are still green.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, open both bags and score the colour of the green bananas.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether a ripe banana can change the green ones near it, and why. 2. Put two green bananas in each bag. 3. Add the ripe banana to one bag and mark that bag R. 4. Fold both bags shut and put them side by side, away from the sun.
flow.say: One bag gets a ripe banana as a neighbour. Will that make any difference to the green ones? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what the ripe banana will do. Fill both bags. Mark the bag with the ripe banana.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ripe Banana Test. Here you guess, and you set up the two bags.
flow.parent: If you cannot get green bananas, firm green tomatoes or raw mangoes work in the same way, but more slowly.

flow.do: 1. Open both bags. 2. Score the colour of the green bananas in each, from 1 to 4. 3. Write the scores down and close the bags.
flow.say: Let's look. What score would you give the green bananas in each bag today?
flow.kid: Open both bags. Score the green bananas from 1 to 4. Write it down. Close the bags.
flow.context: This step of the Ripe Banana Test is the daily look. Here you score the colour of the bananas in each bag.
flow.wait: Do this step once a day on days 2 and 3.

flow.do: 1. Score the bananas one last time. 2. Lay the bananas from the two bags side by side. 3. Ask what your child claims, what they saw and why. 4. Then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Tell me what you found. The bananas never touched a wire or a tube. So how did the ripe one reach the others?
flow.kid: Score the bananas. Put them side by side. Say what happened, and say how you think it happened.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Ripe Banana Test. Here you compare the two bags and explain the difference.
flow.parent: After your child has answered: the green bananas beside the ripe one usually turn yellow a day or two sooner. A ripening banana gives off ethylene, a gas that is a plant hormone. In the closed bag the gas builds up. The green bananas have receptors for it, and they answer by ripening. If both bags look the same, the green bananas may already have begun to ripen and were making their own ethylene.

check.q: How did the ripe banana make its green neighbours ripen sooner?
options: It gave off a hormone gas that they answered
check.why: A ripening banana releases ethylene gas. Cells in the green bananas have receptors for ethylene, and they start to ripen. Choosing 'warmed' is a fair guess, but a ripe banana is not warmer than a green one.

activities.title: One Grain, Ten Grains, a Hundred: act out the chain of command
activities.context: In this activity three people, or one person and two toys, act as the hypothalamus, the pituitary and the thyroid gland. They pass rice grains to stand for hormones. You will see how a tiny signal from the brain grows at each step, and how the last gland tells the first one to stop.

materials.item: uncooked rice, about two tablespoons
small bowls or steel plates
paper slips to label the four places: hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid and body cells
toys or cushions to stand in if there are fewer than three people

activities.record: Draw the chain as four boxes with arrows. Write the number of grains on each arrow. Add the arrow that goes back from the thyroid to the hypothalamus.

setup.art: Four steel plates in a row on the floor, each with a paper label, and a small heap of rice beside the first plate.
setup.caption: 1. Put four labelled plates in a row: hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid and body cells.

setup.art: A girl placing one grain of rice on the second plate, her brother counting out ten grains for the third plate, and a toy elephant sitting beside the third plate.
setup.caption: 2. Pass the message along. One grain becomes ten, and ten become a hundred.

setup.art: A child carrying a small pinch of rice from the last plate back to the first plate, where another child holds up a hand to say stop.
setup.caption: 3. When the body cells have enough, carry a pinch back to the start. The hypothalamus stops.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the four plates and labels. 2. Give each person or toy a role. 3. Explain that a rice grain stands for a tiny amount of hormone.
flow.say: You are the hypothalamus. I am the pituitary. The elephant is the thyroid. Rice grains are our hormones.
flow.kid: Lay out four plates. Choose who is the hypothalamus, the pituitary and the thyroid.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Grain, Ten Grains, a Hundred. Here you set out the plates and choose roles.

flow.do: 1. The hypothalamus puts 1 grain on the pituitary's plate. 2. For each grain it gets, the pituitary puts 10 grains on the thyroid's plate. 3. For each grain it gets, the thyroid puts 10 grains on the body cells' plate. 4. Count what the body cells received. 5. Repeat with 2 grains at the start.
flow.say: I got one grain, so I send ten. The thyroid got ten, so the thyroid sends a hundred. How many would two grains make?
flow.kid: Send one grain. The next gland sends ten for each grain. Count what arrives at the end.
flow.context: This step of One Grain, Ten Grains, a Hundred passes the signal down the chain and watches it grow.

ask.q: Why might a body be built so that each step sends out more than it received?
good: The brain only has to make a tiny amount.
A small change at the top makes a big change at the bottom.

flow.parent: The numbers are for the game only. In a real body each step does release more hormone than the step before, but not in neat tens.

flow.do: 1. Start again, and let the hypothalamus send 1 grain every ten seconds. 2. When the body cells' plate holds 300 grains, carry a pinch from it back to the hypothalamus. 3. The hypothalamus then stops sending. 4. Ask what would happen with no message back.
flow.say: The body cells have enough now. Some of their hormone travels back to the start. What should the hypothalamus do?
flow.kid: Keep sending grains. When the last plate is full, carry a pinch back. Then stop sending.
flow.context: This is the last step of One Grain, Ten Grains, a Hundred. Here the last gland's hormone goes back and stops the first.

check.q: The pituitary is sometimes called the 'master gland'. What did this activity show about that name?
options: It is right, because the pituitary starts everything
It is only partly right, because the pituitary takes orders too
It is wrong, because the pituitary makes no hormones
check.why: The pituitary does drive other glands. But it acts on a signal from the hypothalamus, and it eases off when the thyroid's hormone comes back. Choosing the first answer may mean looking at one arrow of the chain and not the whole circle.

projects.title: My Growth Curve: how fast have I been growing?
projects.context: In this project you measure your height carefully, hunt for your old heights in health cards, school reports and pencil marks on a door frame, and draw them all as one line graph. You will work out how many centimetres you have grown each year, and compare that with what growth hormone usually manages.

materials.item: a wall with a hard floor in front of it
a hardback book and a pencil
a measuring tape or a metre scale
old height records: a health or vaccination card, school report cards or door-frame marks
graph paper or squared paper from a maths notebook

schedule.what: Measure your height. Collect your old heights with their dates. Draw a line graph and work out your growth in each year.

projects.record: Make a table of your age and your height each time it was measured. Draw the line graph. Under it, write how many centimetres you grew in each full year. Mark today's date on a calendar three months from now, to measure again.

setup.art: A girl standing barefoot with her heels, back and head against a wall, looking straight ahead, while her mother holds a hardback book flat on her head with its edge against the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Stand barefoot against a wall. A helper rests a book flat on your head and marks the wall under it.

setup.art: A measuring tape held from the floor up to a small pencil mark on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Measure from the floor to the mark, to the nearest half centimetre.

setup.art: A health card, a school report card and a door frame with dated pencil marks, beside a sheet of graph paper with a rising line of dots.
setup.caption: 3. Collect your old heights and their dates. Plot them all on one graph.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands barefoot with heels, back and head touching the wall, looking straight ahead. 2. Rest a hardback book flat on the head, with one edge against the wall. 3. Mark the wall lightly under the book. 4. Measure from floor to mark. 5. Do it three times and take the middle value.
flow.say: Stand tall but do not stretch. I will mark the wall under the book. We measure three times, because one try can be a little off.
flow.kid: Stand barefoot against the wall. Look straight ahead. Your helper marks your height three times.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Growth Curve. Here you measure your height today as exactly as you can.
flow.parent: Measure at the same time of day as you will next time. Everyone is a little taller in the morning than in the evening.

flow.do: 1. Look for old heights in health cards, school reports and door-frame marks. 2. Write each height with its date. 3. Work out your child's age at each date, in years and months. 4. Before plotting, ask what shape the line will have, and why.
flow.say: Let's find every height anyone ever wrote down for you. What shape do you think the line will make? Why?
flow.kid: Find your old heights and their dates. Work out your age each time. Guess the shape of the line.
flow.context: This step of My Growth Curve collects your old heights and your age at each one.

ask.q: What shape do you think the line will make, and why?
good: A straight slope, because I grow a bit every year.
Steep at first, because babies grow very fast, and then less steep.

flow.parent: If you find no old records, plot today's height as the first point and use the made-up example in the maths cards for practice. Then measure every three months.

flow.do: 1. Draw age along the bottom of the graph and height up the side. 2. Plot each height and join the points. 3. For each full year, subtract to find the centimetres grown. 4. Ask what the graph shows. 5. Then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Tell me what your graph shows. In which year did you grow most? How many centimetres do you grow in a usual year?
flow.kid: Plot your heights. Join the points. Work out how much you grew each year. Say what you see.
flow.context: This is the last step of My Growth Curve. Here you draw the graph and work out your growth in each year.
flow.parent: After your child has answered: from about age 4 until puberty most children grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year, which is about half a centimetre a month. Babies grow far faster. In puberty the line turns steeper again for a few years, and then goes flat when the growth plates close. Old records are often rough, so a year that looks odd may be a measuring slip. Children grow at different speeds and at different ages, and a wide range is healthy.

check.q: A girl's height line goes flat at 16 and stays flat. What has happened in her bones?
options: Her growth plates have turned to bone
check.why: At the end of puberty, oestrogen makes the cartilage of the growth plates turn to bone, so the long bones can no longer lengthen. The pituitary goes on making growth hormone all through life. Choosing 'pituitary' may mean thinking growth hormone is the only thing that decides height.

challenges.title: Slow Release: make a colour keep coming for ten minutes
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. Some glands release their hormone little by little, and doctors design medicines that do the same. Here you build something that lets colour into a tumbler of still water slowly and steadily, and not all at once.
challenges.problem: Put colour into a clear tumbler of still water so that colour starts to come out within one minute and is still clearly coming out ten minutes later.
constraints: After you start the timer, nobody may touch, stir or shake the tumbler.
The colour must begin to show within one minute.
New colour must still be seen leaving your device at ten minutes.
Use only things from the house.
materials: clear glass tumblers or cut-down clear plastic bottles, and water
a strong colour: food colouring, ink, beetroot juice or very strong tea
an ice tray and a freezer, if you have one
kitchen foil, cotton wool, a strip of thick cloth, thread and a pin
a tea bag, a slice of raw potato or carrot
general: Freeze the colour into an ice cube the night before. The cube melts slowly and lets the colour out as it melts.
Soak cotton wool in colour and wrap it tightly in foil. Prick one small hole with a pin. Colour leaks out through the hole.
Use a tea bag. Its paper lets colour through slowly, which is what it was made for.
creative: Hang a strip of thick cloth soaked in colour so that only its tip touches the water. The colour creeps down the cloth.
Stir the colour into a spoon of thick sugar syrup and lower the spoon to the bottom. The heavy syrup sits there and the colour rises from it slowly.
Scoop a small hollow in a slice of raw potato, fill it with colour and cover it with a second slice held on by thread.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Run it beside a tumbler in which you put one drop of colour straight in. Which one is like adrenaline in a fright, and which is like a medicine patch that works all day?

setup.art: Two clear glass tumblers of water on a table, with a bottle of food colouring, a pin, foil, cotton wool, a tea bag and an ice tray laid out beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill two clear tumblers with water. Collect a colour and things to hold it back.

setup.art: One tumbler with a single drop of red colour spreading through the water in a quick cloud, and a second tumbler with a small foil packet at the bottom leaking a thin thread of red.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop straight into the first tumbler. Lower your device into the second. Start the timer and do not touch.

flow.do: 1. Fill two clear tumblers with water and let them stand until still. 2. Put one drop of colour straight into the first and watch for a minute. 3. Read the problem and its limits aloud.
flow.say: That is what colour does with nothing to hold it back. Your job is to make it keep coming for ten minutes.
flow.kid: Put one drop of colour in still water. Watch it spread. Then read the rules of the challenge.
flow.context: This is the first step of Slow Release. Here you see how fast colour spreads when nothing holds it back.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to sketch two ideas before building. 2. Build one. 3. Lower it into the second tumbler and start the timer. 4. Look at 1 minute, 5 minutes and 10 minutes without touching.
flow.say: Sketch two ideas first. What will hold the colour back? What will let a little of it out?
flow.kid: Sketch two ideas. Build one. Lower it in and start the timer. Do not touch the tumbler.
flow.context: This step of Slow Release is for designing, building and timing your device.
flow.parent: The usual failure is a hole that is too big, so everything comes out in the first minute. Let your child find this out and try a smaller hole.

flow.do: 1. Change one thing in the design and test again in fresh water. 2. Compare the two runs. 3. Ask which body messages need a quick burst and which need a slow, steady supply.
flow.say: Change one thing and test again. Then tell me: which hormone in your body comes in a quick burst, and which comes slowly all night?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again in fresh water. Say which design worked better and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of Slow Release. Here you improve your design and link it to hormones.

check.q: Which hormone is released in a quick burst that fades within minutes?
check.why: Adrenaline is released within seconds and cleared within minutes, like the drop of colour. Melatonin is released steadily for the whole night, and thyroid hormone is kept at a steady level for weeks. Choosing another answer may mean thinking all hormones act at one speed.

challenges.title: The Jet-Lag Planner: move a body clock from Chennai to London
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. A body clock can be moved only about an hour a day, and light is the main thing that moves it. Here you plan how a traveller can use light and dark to shift her clock before and after a long flight west.
challenges.problem: Dr Revathi flies from Chennai to London on Saturday. London is 5 and a half hours behind Chennai in winter. Plan her light, dark, sleep and meals from Wednesday to the following Tuesday, so that she is sleepy at London bedtime as soon as possible.
constraints: She works in Chennai from 9 in the morning to 5 in the evening until Friday.
She takes no sleep tablets and no melatonin tablets.
Her clock can move by about one hour a day, and not more.
She needs about eight hours of sleep each night.
materials: two long strips of paper, each marked with the 24 hours of a day
a ruler, a pencil and two colour pencils
a sheet of paper for the plan
general: From Wednesday, go to bed one hour later each night and wake one hour later where work allows. Each day the clock moves a little towards London time.
Seek bright light in the evening, because evening light pushes the clock later. Stay in dim light for the first hour after waking.
In London, spend the afternoon and early evening outdoors, so that daylight keeps pushing the clock later.
creative: Eat meals at London times from Friday, because the clocks in the liver and gut take their time from food.
On the plane, sleep only when it is night in London, and keep the window shade open when it is day there.
Wear dark glasses on the bright morning drive to work in the last days, to keep morning light from pulling the clock back.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan the flight home, from London east to Chennai. The clock must move earlier this time. Which light must she seek, and which must she avoid? Why do many travellers find flying east harder?

setup.art: Two long paper strips laid one above the other on a table, each marked with 24 hours, the lower strip slid five and a half hours to the right of the upper one, labelled Chennai and London.
setup.caption: 1. Make two 24-hour strips, one for Chennai time and one for London time. Slide one so that the hours match.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with seven rows for seven days, each row showing a yellow bar for bright light, a grey bar for dim light and a blue bar for sleep, shifting a little to the right each day.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one row for each day. Colour in when she sleeps and when she seeks bright light.

flow.do: 1. Mark 24 hours along each paper strip. 2. Label one Chennai and one London. 3. Slide the London strip so that midnight in London sits under 5:30 in the morning in Chennai. 4. Read the problem and its limits aloud.
flow.say: When it is bedtime in London, what time does her body think it is? Use the strips to find out.
flow.kid: Make two strips of 24 hours. Slide one by five and a half hours. Read the problem.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Jet-Lag Planner. Here you make two time strips and see how far the clock must move.

ask.q: At 10 at night in London, what time is it on her Chennai body clock?
good: Half past three in the morning.
Her body thinks the night is nearly over.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the two rules about light, from the parent note. 2. Draw seven rows, one for each day. 3. Your child colours in sleep, bright light and dim light for each day. 4. Check each row against the limits.
flow.say: Light in the body's evening pushes the clock later. Light in the body's morning pulls it earlier. Which does she need?
flow.kid: Draw a row for each day. Colour in sleep, bright light and dim light. Check the rules.
flow.context: This step of the Jet-Lag Planner is for drawing the plan, one row for each day.
flow.parent: The two rules: bright light in the hours before the body's usual bedtime moves the clock later. Bright light in the hours after the body's usual waking time moves it earlier. Flying west, she needs her clock to move later.

flow.do: 1. Your child explains the plan day by day. 2. Count how many days pass before her body's bedtime matches London's. 3. Ask the check question. 4. Start the 'your turn' plan for the flight home.
flow.say: Talk me through your plan. On which day does her body's bedtime match London's?
flow.kid: Explain your plan day by day. Count the days until her clock matches London.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Jet-Lag Planner. Here you explain your plan and count how long the shift takes.

check.q: A traveller wants her body clock to move later. When should she seek bright light?
check.why: Bright light in the evening tells the clock that the day is still going, so the clock shifts later and melatonin comes later. Morning light does the opposite. Choosing 'no difference' may mean thinking light only helps you see.

worksheets.title: Hormones, glands and three jobs: alarm, growth and sleep (core)

items.p: What is a hormone?
opts: An electrical signal along a nerve
A chemical message carried in the blood
items.why: A hormone is a chemical that cells release into the blood. It changes what certain other cells do. Choosing 'electrical signal' mixes it up with a nerve message.

items.p: The glands that release hormones into the blood make up the ____ system.
a: endocrine
items.why: The endocrine system is all the glands and cells that make hormones, taken together.

items.p: Match each gland to one hormone that it makes.
pairs: Inner part of the adrenal glands
items.why: Each gland releases its own hormones. The pituitary also makes hormones that drive other glands.

items.p: True or false: a hormone changes every cell that it reaches.
items.why: False. A hormone reaches nearly every cell, because blood goes everywhere. Only cells with the receptor for that hormone answer it.

items.p: In the Alarm Test your pulse rose while you sat still. What started the rise?
opts: Your brain judging the task urgent
items.why: No big muscle was working. The brain judged the race against the timer to be urgent and sent signals to the heart and the adrenal glands.

items.p: Put these in order, for what happens in a fright.
a: The brain judges that something is urgent
Nerves signal the heart and the adrenal glands
The heart speeds up within about a second
Adrenaline enters the blood and keeps the heart fast
The body breaks the adrenaline down over a few minutes
items.why: Nerves act first because a nerve signal arrives in a fraction of a second. Adrenaline follows within seconds and lasts until it is broken down.

items.p: In an alarm, does each of these go up or go down?
items: heart rate
Goes up
width of the airways
Goes up
glucose in the blood
Goes up
saliva in the mouth
Goes down
blood flow to the gut
Goes down
blood flow to the big muscles
Goes up
items.why: The alarm sends fuel and blood to the heart, lungs and big muscles. Jobs that can wait, such as digesting, are turned down.

items.p: A bang lasts one second, but your heart thumps for a minute or more. Explain why.
items.a: The nerve signal stops quickly. But adrenaline has been released into my blood. It keeps acting on my heart until my body has broken it down, and that takes a few minutes.
items.why: A strong answer says that the hormone stays in the blood after the event is over, and that clearing it takes time.

items.p: Where does a child's leg bone get longer?
opts: In the hard middle of the bone
At the growth plates near its ends
items.why: The growth plates are thin layers of cartilage near each end of a long bone. Cartilage cells divide there, and bone replaces the cartilage.

items.p: The thyroid gland cannot make its hormone without the element ____.
a: iodine
items.why: Each molecule of thyroid hormone holds three or four iodine atoms. That is why salt is iodised.

items.p: True or false: the pineal gland makes most of its melatonin in bright daylight.
items.why: False. Melatonin is made in the dark. Bright light holds it back.

items.p: Which two things together set the time you feel sleepy?
opts: The body clock and sleep pressure
items.why: The body clock sends the night signal, melatonin. Sleep pressure builds up the longer you stay awake. Sleepiness depends on both.

items.p: Draw a body outline. Mark and label five hormone glands in the right places.
items.a: An outline showing any five of these: hypothalamus and pituitary under the brain, pineal gland in the middle of the brain, thyroid at the front of the neck, adrenal glands on top of the kidneys, pancreas behind the stomach, ovaries or testes low down.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the glands in the right places and shows how small they are compared with the body.

items.p: In Ten Times Weaker, tumbler 4 tasted like plain water. Is there sugar in it? How do you know?
items.a: Yes. I put one spoon from tumbler 3 into it, and tumbler 3 had sugar. Sugar does not vanish when it is diluted. My tongue's receptors need more sugar than that before they answer.
items.why: A strong answer separates what is there from what the tongue can detect.

items.p: Name one thing your body did today that a hormone helped to control. Name the hormone and its gland.
items.a: Answers vary. For example: I got sleepy last night. Melatonin from my pineal gland helped. Or: I grew a tiny bit. Growth hormone from my pituitary helped. Or: my heart raced before the match. Adrenaline from my adrenal glands helped.
items.why: Any true example with the right hormone and gland is a strong answer.

worksheets.title: Receptors, the chain of command and timing (stretch)

items.p: Adrenaline speeds up heart muscle and relaxes gut muscle. Why do the two answer differently?
opts: There are two kinds of adrenaline
The gut gets a weaker dose
items.why: It is one chemical. Heart cells and gut muscle cells carry different kinds of adrenaline receptor, and each kind starts a different chain inside the cell.

items.p: True or false: the pituitary gland gives orders but never takes any.
items.why: False. The pituitary acts on releasing hormones from the hypothalamus. It also eases off when hormones from the glands it drives come back to it.

items.p: Put these in order, for how the thyroid is told to work.
a: The hypothalamus sends a releasing hormone
The pituitary releases its hormone into the blood
The thyroid gland makes more thyroid hormone
Thyroid hormone reaches cells all over the body
Thyroid hormone tells the hypothalamus and pituitary to ease off
items.why: The order runs from brain to pituitary to thyroid, and then the thyroid's own hormone goes back to slow the first two. The chain is a circle.

items.p: The time the body takes to clear half of a hormone from the blood is called its ____.
a: half-life
half life
items.why: A hormone with a short half-life gives a short message. Adrenaline's is a few minutes.

items.p: In Clear the Alarm you start with 32 tokens. Half go each round. How many are left after 3 rounds?
items.why: 32 becomes 16, then 8, then 4. Each round takes away half of what is left, so the amount removed gets smaller each time.

items.p: Match each hormone to the time when its level is highest.
pairs: during a fright or a race
items.why: Each hormone has its own timing. Some follow the body clock, some follow sleep, and some follow events.

items.p: Does each hormone join a receptor on the outside of the cell, or go inside?
cats: Joins a receptor on the outside
items: adrenaline
Joins a receptor on the outside
insulin
Joins a receptor on the outside
growth hormone
Joins a receptor on the outside
cortisol
Goes inside and switches genes
oestrogen
Goes inside and switches genes
thyroid hormone
Goes inside and switches genes
items.why: Steroid hormones and thyroid hormone enter the cell and act on genes, which is slow and lasting. The others stay outside and act through receptors on the cell's surface, which is quick.

items.p: Insulin must be injected, but thyroid hormone can be swallowed as a tablet. Explain why.
items.a: Insulin is a protein. The stomach and gut would digest it like food before it reached the blood. Thyroid hormone is a small, tough molecule that survives digestion and passes into the blood.
items.why: A strong answer says what kind of molecule each one is and what the gut does to proteins.

items.p: In the Dim Evening Test, what was the one thing changed on purpose?
opts: The brightness of the room light
items.why: Only the room light differed between the two kinds of evening. Dinner, lights-off time, screens and activities were kept the same, so that any difference could be put down to the light.

items.p: In the Dim Evening Test you knew which evenings were dim. Explain how that could change your sleepiness scores.
items.a: I expected to feel sleepy on dim evenings, so I may have given a higher score without meaning to. The minutes to fall asleep are a fairer measure, because someone else measured them.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a person who knows what is being tested can shift their own scores, and names a measure that is harder to shift.

items.p: True or false: boys' bodies make no oestrogen.
items.why: False. Boys make oestrogen in smaller amounts than girls. It is the hormone that closes the growth plates in both.

items.p: Draw the shape of a line graph of one person's height from birth to age 20. Label four parts.
items.a: A line that rises very steeply in the first two years, then rises steadily through childhood, then rises more steeply for a few years in puberty, and then goes flat.
items.why: A strong drawing has four parts: fast baby growth, steady childhood growth, the puberty spurt, and the flat line after the growth plates close.

items.p: A long afternoon nap makes you less sleepy at bedtime. What has the nap changed?
items.why: Sleep pressure builds while you are awake and falls while you sleep. The nap lowered it. The body clock and melatonin still run on time.

items.p: Two views about what melatonin is.

views.who: A label on a bottle of tablets
views.says: Melatonin is the sleep hormone. When it rises, people get sleepy.
Melatonin is a darkness signal. A rat's melatonin rises at night too, and that is when rats wake up.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give a reason from this lesson.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For the scientist: the same hormone rises at night in animals that sleep then and in animals that wake then. For the label: in humans, sleepiness does follow the evening rise.
items.why: Both statements are true of some animals. The second explains more, because it fits day-active and night-active animals alike.

items.p: The colour of light that most affects the body clock is ____.
a: blue
items.why: The special cells in the eye that report to the body clock are most affected by blue light. Daylight and white tube lights hold a lot of it.

items.p: One adrenaline molecule can lead to thousands of glucose molecules leaving a liver cell. What is this called?
items.why: Each step in the chain inside the cell switches on many molecules of the next step. So a tiny signal becomes a big effect.

items.p: The Alarm Test cannot separate nerves from adrenaline. What extra measurement could?
items.a: A blood sample taken at rest and during the race, to measure how much adrenaline is in the blood each time. Scientists have done this, and found that adrenaline about doubles but stays low.
items.why: A strong answer names something that measures the hormone itself, and not only the heart.

items.p: True or false: plants make hormones.
items.why: True. Auxin makes shoots bend to light, and ethylene gas ripens fruit. Plants have no blood, so their hormones travel in sap or through the air.

items.p: Put these in order, for how your body gets its night signal.
a: The light fades in the evening
Cells in the eye report less brightness to the body clock
The body clock lets the pineal gland start work
The pineal gland releases melatonin into the blood
Organs all over the body get the message that it is night
items.why: The message begins as light, becomes a nerve signal and ends as a hormone that reaches every organ.

items.p: A man was still growing taller at 28. His body made all its hormones. What was missing?
items.why: Oestrogen closes the growth plates. His cells had no working receptor for it, so the message was sent and never received. This shows that a hormone does nothing without its receptor.

items.p: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.
pairs: Tadpoles fed thyroid gland became frogs early
People in rooms with no clocks kept a daily rhythm
the body clock runs by itself
Villages given iodised salt had fewer goitres
Bright light at night lowered melatonin in the blood
A ripe banana in a bag ripened the green ones
a hormone can travel as a gas
items.why: Each idea in this lesson rests on a test that someone carried out. The evidence comes first and the idea follows.

items.p: Would each of these move a body clock later or earlier?
items: bright light late in the evening
Moves the clock later
bright light just after waking
Moves the clock earlier
staying outdoors until sunset after flying west
Moves the clock later
opening the curtains at sunrise
Moves the clock earlier
items.why: Light in the body's evening tells the clock that the day is still going. Light in the body's morning tells it that the day has begun.

items.p: Thyroid hormone lengthens a child's bones and makes a tadpole's tail shrink away. What does this tell you about hormones?
items.a: The hormone is the same molecule in both. It does not carry the instruction 'grow' or 'shrink'. Each kind of cell answers in the way that cell is built to answer. So the meaning of a hormone is decided by the cell that receives it.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same message gets different answers, and that the difference lies in the receiving cell.

items.p: A tadpole in a drying pool becomes a toad early and small. What kind of signal times the change?
opts: A hormone that answers news from outside
A reflex through the spinal cord
The tadpole's age and nothing else
items.why: Thyroid hormone drives the change, and falling water makes it rise sooner. So the body uses a hormone to fit its timing to the world outside.

items.p: Two views about fear and a pounding heart.

views.says: The body changes first. We feel afraid because we sense our heart pounding and our hands trembling.
The feeling comes first. I see the danger, I feel afraid, and then my heart pounds because I am afraid.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Use what you noticed in the Alarm Test, or in a real fright.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives something the child noticed. For James: my heart was already fast before I knew I was nervous. For the common view: I was worried about the sums first, and my pulse rose after.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. What matters is that the reason comes from something observed.

items.p: A cycle of about one day in a living body is called a ____ rhythm.
a: circadian
items.why: 'Circadian' comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day'. Sleep, body temperature, melatonin and cortisol all follow circadian rhythms.

items.p: Your bars for bright and dim evenings come out equal. Give two reasons why light might still matter for sleep.
items.a: Three evenings of each kind is too few, so one odd day could hide a real difference. Our bright light may not have been bright enough, or our dim light not dim enough, to change melatonin. A different child might also answer light more strongly.
items.why: A strong answer does not jump from 'no difference in my test' to 'no effect at all'. It names a limit of the test.

items.p: Draw how one hormone molecule outside a cell leads to many molecules leaving the cell.
items.a: A cell with one hormone molecule on a receptor in its outer skin. Inside, the receptor switches on a few helper proteins, each helper makes many small messenger molecules, these switch on enzymes, and many glucose molecules leave the cell.
items.why: A strong drawing gets wider at each step, like a fan, and keeps the hormone outside the cell.

items.p: The human body clock runs about 11 minutes slow each day. What sets it right?
items.why: Light reaching special cells in the eye resets the clock each morning. People who cannot get this light signal often drift a little later every day.

items.p: True or false: an asthma inhaler works because its medicine fits one kind of adrenaline receptor.
items.why: True. The medicine is shaped to fit the kind of adrenaline receptor found on the muscle round the airways. That muscle relaxes and the airways open, with less effect on other organs.

quiz.why: The pineal gland, the size of a grain of rice in the middle of the brain, makes melatonin in the dark. Choosing 'thyroid' mixes up the night signal with the hormone that sets the pace of cells.

opts: At the front of the neck
quiz.why: One adrenal gland sits on top of each kidney. The thyroid is in the neck, and the pituitary is under the brain.

quiz.p: After a fright, why does your heart thump for a minute or more?
opts: Adrenaline stays in the blood until it is broken down
quiz.why: Nerve signals stop quickly, but adrenaline keeps acting until the body has cleared it, which takes a few minutes. Choosing 'danger is still there' forgets that the thumping goes on after the danger has gone.

quiz.p: In an alarm, which message reaches the heart first?
quiz.why: A nerve signal arrives in a fraction of a second. Adrenaline must be released and carried round in the blood, which takes some seconds. The two then work together.

quiz.p: Why does a hormone change some cells and not others?
opts: The blood takes it to only some cells
Only some cells have its receptor
quiz.why: Blood carries the hormone nearly everywhere. A cell answers only if it carries the receptor that the hormone fits. Choosing 'blood takes it to only some cells' pictures a hormone as travelling like a nerve signal.

quiz.p: True or false: one hormone can make one kind of cell do more and another kind do less.
quiz.why: True. Adrenaline makes heart muscle work harder and makes gut muscle relax. The answer depends on the receptor and on the cell.

quiz.p: What ends a person's growth in height?
opts: The pituitary stops making growth hormone
The growth plates turn to bone
quiz.why: At the end of puberty, oestrogen makes the cartilage of the growth plates turn to bone. Growth hormone goes on being made all through life.

quiz.p: What does bright light late in the evening do to melatonin?
quiz.why: Bright light tells the body clock that it is still day, so the pineal gland holds back melatonin. Choosing 'rise sooner' has the signal the wrong way round. Melatonin is made in the dark.

quiz.p: You have been awake for 16 hours. What has been building up all that time?
quiz.why: Sleep pressure rises the longer you are awake and falls while you sleep. It is separate from the body clock.

quiz.p: Which part of the brain sends releasing hormones to the pituitary?
quiz.why: The hypothalamus sits just above the pituitary and sends releasing hormones down a short stalk. This is why 'master gland' is only partly right for the pituitary.

quiz.p: How can a tiny amount of a hormone have a big effect?
quiz.why: A receptor that has caught one hormone molecule starts a chain inside the cell, and each step switches on many molecules of the next. Glands are small, and hormones act in tiny amounts.

quiz.p: In a fair test of evening light and sleep, what should differ between the two kinds of evening?
quiz.why: If only the light differs, any change in sleepiness can be put down to the light. If bedtime changed too, you could not tell which one made the difference.
